title: Predictable Timing Enhances the Use of Predictable Content
abstract: As events unfold, they carry structure in both their timing and content, with these dimensions often interrelated. Most research has treated these dimensions separately, although processing them jointly may provide important computational benefits. It is an open question whether the brain processes a sequence's timing and predictable content structure independently, or integrates these two sources of information to guide prediction. We hypothesised that predictable timing would allow listeners to better exploit structure in the content, with this effect increasing as content structure becomes stronger. To test this, we presented tone sequences with pitch trajectories following a 1/f^{beta} structure, where {beta} determines how strongly the content of each tone persists, while independently varying the temporal periodicity of the sequence. Performance was quantified using response errors relative to outcome predictions of a Gaussian Process Regression model and a model-free measure of how strongly preceding tones influenced responses. Response error decreased and reliance on preceding tones increased with higher {beta} and periodic timing. Moreover, the influence of preceding tones showed an interaction between timing and content, such that the effect of periodicity grew with increasing {beta}. The response error showed no such interaction, although the effect of periodic timing was reliable only for the most structured sequences. Our findings suggest an interdependency between content and timing, where predictable timing helps listeners make greater use of predictable content.

title: Chronic unpredictable stress induces negative cognitive bias in rats with sex-specific changes in neurogenesis and functional connectivity
abstract: Background: Females are more likely to be diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) than males. Cognitive symptoms of MDD include negative cognitive bias, the perception of ambiguous situations as negative, which predicts MDD episode onset and severity. MDD is associated with changes to functional connectivity between regions involved in cognition, emotion, attention, and memory. Methods: Here we examined the impact of chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) on negative cognitive bias in male (n=18) and female (n=22) Sprague-Dawley rats. We assessed hippocampal neurogenesis and c-Fos expression in response to an ambiguous context across 15 regions of the frontal cortex, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, including in newborn dentate gyrus (DG) neurons, to examine functional connectivity during cognitive bias testing. We conducted a graph-based network analysis and constructed linear models to predict freezing in the ambiguous context based on regional activation. Results: CUS-exposed rats froze more to the ambiguous context than non-CUS-exposed rats, regardless of sex. CUS decreased neurogenesis in the ventral DG of both sexes, and increased activation of new neurons in the dorsal DG of males only. In response to the ambiguous context, CUS males had an increase in c-Fos expression in the amygdala. CUS produced extensive, sex-specific network reorganization, decreasing global network efficiency in males but not in females. Freezing in the ambiguous context was predicted by activation of new neurons in combination with the ventral CA1 in opposing directions across sex. Conclusions: These findings suggest that sex-specific pathways drive the expression of CUS-induced negative cognitive bias, underscoring the necessity of sex-stratified preclinical and clinical research on negative cognitive bias in depression.

title: Fixel-wise Differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter
abstract: Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC).Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3 - 13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts.FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group by Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering.

title: Multimodal profiling and intersectional genetics reveal CA1 border inhibitory neuron diversity and postnatal emergence of retrosplenial connectivity
abstract: Inhibitory neurons (INs) at the stratum radiatum/stratum lacunosum-moleculare border of hippocampal CA1 comprise diverse populations, including long-range-projecting neurons that innervate the retrosplenial cortex (RSCtx). However, their molecular organization and developmental connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine multimodal transcriptomic profiling, intersectional genetics, and retrograde tracing to characterize CA1 border INs. We identified two major caudal ganglionic eminence-derived, Cxcl14-enriched populations distinguished by Syt6/Cck-related and Ntng1-expressing transcriptional profiles. We then generated a Cxcl14-Cre mouse line that, when combined with an IN-specific viral enhancer, provides genetic access to CA1 border INs. Retrograde labeling established that  CA1 INs projecting to the RSCtx belong to the Ntng1-expressing population, and that this long-range projection emerges during postnatal mouse development, between postnatal days 3 and 5. Finally, analysis of genes encoding cell-surface proteins, key regulators of connectivity, revealed distinct expression profiles in RSCtx-projecting and SYT6-positive INs. Together, these findings establish a molecular and developmental framework for CA1 border IN diversity and provide a genetic strategy for investigating the assembly and function of these inhibitory circuits.

title: MRI-free OPM-MEG recovers medial temporal lobe theta during scene imagination
abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) offers a wearable, movement-tolerant alternative to conventional cryogenic MEG, placing sensors closer to the scalp and, in principle, improving sensitivity to deep sources. This is advantageous for examining subcortical structures that are affected by ageing, disorders and disease, such as the hippocampus. However, it remains unclear whether well-established activity (such as the attenuation of theta oscillations during the imagination of novel scenes) can be recovered from the medial temporal lobe (MTL) with OPM-MEG, and whether an individual structural MRI is required. Here, fifteen adults completed a scene imagination task. Initially we applied a 12-parameter template warping coregistration pipeline to the full sample. Following source reconstruction, we recovered the expected attenuation of theta (4-8 Hz) power during scene imagination compared to a counting baseline, with a significant cluster of activity peaking in the left parahippocampal gyrus. The clusters centre of mass was localised to the left hippocampus (t = -3.55, p = 0.048, whole-brain FWE-corrected) and was mostly confined to the left medial temporal lobe. We further supported our findings by using an individual T1-weighted MRI reconstruction pipeline in six participants who had these scans available. The two approaches produced similar whole-brain topographies and localised the peak MTL theta effect to left hippocampus, with temporal-lobe conjunction centroids 3-mm apart. These findings provide evidence that the theta attenuation of the scene construction network can be recovered at the group level with OPM-MEG, without an individual MRI.

title: Conserved Laminar-Cellular Architecture Predicts the Spectrolaminar Motif
abstract: We recently identified the spectrolaminar motif, a layer-resolved pattern of local field potential (LFP) power, which is preserved across many areas of the primate cortex. It remains unclear which specific cytoarchitectonic features can explain the spectrolaminar motif. To investigate this, we performed histological and neurophysiological analyses of 11 brain areas spanning the macaque cortical hierarchy to examine the relationship between the laminar patterns of LFP power and the laminar distributions of cellular density for parvalbumin, calbindin, and calretinin interneurons, and pyramidal neurons. We tested whether cellular distributions are conserved and if they predict the corresponding variation in LFP power comprising the spectrolaminar motif. We found that the cytoarchitectonic and spectrolaminar data were intrinsically low-dimensional, with two-component patterns conserved across areas, and that the spectrolaminar motif could be predicted from these laminar cellular gradients. Critically, the regression coefficients mapping structure (cytoarchitecture) to function (spectrolaminar motif) were themselves highly conserved across areas, suggesting that a common cellular-to-spectral rule operates throughout cortex rather than a distinct rule per region. To evaluate this structure-function model, we tested it against post-mortem data from schizophrenia patients. We tested whether empirically-observed cytoarchitectonic changes from postmortem studies on inhibitory interneuron dysfunction in schizophrenia could be used to predict spectrolaminar alterations using our structure-function model. We found that they did, and that the functional changes match what is known from non-invasive neurophysiology in schizophrenia. This work moves beyond simple structure-function correlation to establish a predictive mathematical framework that informs healthy and aberrant brain circuitry.

title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling
abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.

title: Structural plasticity and enhanced fear extinction following psilocybin in chronically stressed mice
abstract: The classic psychedelic psilocybin elicits long-lasting neural plasticity and behavioral effects, but prior studies largely examined stress-naive animals. Using longitudinal imaging, we show that psilocybin increases dendritic spine density in frontal cortical neurons and facilitates fear extinction after chronic restraint stress, demonstrating psilocybin's effects in a translationally relevant mouse model.

title: Auditory-motor interactions are sensitive to adaptation and learning on multiple timescales
abstract: Auditory-motor learning is critical for mastering the production of complex sounds, such as speaking and playing music. It is anchored upon internal models of interactions between actions and their sensory consequences, which are fine-tuned by minimizing the errors between the predicted and received sound. Here, we investigated the neural dynamics of sensorimotor learning by manipulating sensorimotor surprisal, with high surprisal defined as unexpected changes in the mapping between actions and their auditory outcomes. Participants performed a piano-playing task in which the key-to-pitch mapping switched unpredictably among three configurations, creating a dynamic sensorimotor environment that required ongoing adaptation. At the change boundaries, a signature of violated motor-to-auditory predictions was found in the auditory evoked responses at N100, which could not be attributed to either purely auditory surprisals or motor execution errors. This prediction error is modulated by short-term context, with greater error responses following longer periods of no map change, indicating that the brain continuously tracks short-term map contexts and rapidly adapts to them. In contrast, 30 minutes of extended goal-directed training on a single key-pitch map modulated P50 amplitude only for the trained map, a modulation that can be explained by a slow, training-driven update of the sensorimotor map. Hence, while auditory predictions from motor actions can be implicitly learned within short-term contexts for rapid adaptation, the complementary process of building a reliable sensorimotor map requires targeted training sustained over time. Our approach of studying auditory-motor surprisal in time-varying sequences reveals that auditory-motor learning is fast, context-sensitive, and shaped by both short- and long-term experience.

title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory
abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but helps construct the representations that are subsequently stored and retrieved. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixation-dependent samples are integrated into an evolving internal representation before one-shot storage in associative memory. Within individual elements, successive samples progressively individuate the representation; across elements, transitions promote relational integration. Crucially, both effects arise from the same history-dependent updating process where each new sample is integrated into a state already shaped by what came before. As a result, sampling history becomes embedded in the memory representation itself. Changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the resulting representation and element-specific retrieval, while reinstating the original sampling trajectory facilitates access to the stored memory. Model-neural analysis further show that changes in the model's evolving representations correspond to neural representational dynamics in lateral temporal cortex. Together, these findings support sequential sampling as a candidate computational process for constructing representations available to episodic memory, linking ongoing perceptual sampling to subsequent memory formation and retrieval.

title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study
abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-unique predictive information in superior temporal regions and a separate frontal-pole interaction, Follower-unique predictive information in insular and superior frontal regions, sparse Synergy in the right rostral anterior cingulate cortex, and Redundancy spanning multiple cortical regions. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides a scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.

abstract: Achieving single-cell detection with electrochemical cytosensors remains challenging, owing to a poor understanding of how electroactive redox probes generate measurable signals near large, insulating cells. Here, we validate a cell–electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in situ visualizing that the measurable current signal originating from redox probes located at the cell–electrode adjacent interface, rather than from those distributed on the cell surface. Notably, cell spreading enlarges this cell-adjacent interface, thereby enabling effective current amplification. Guided by this effect, we design an integrated cytosensor platform that combines a highly conductive lamellar reduced graphene oxide (RGO)/Ti 3 C 2 T x electrode chip, which facilitates lamellipodia-driven cell spreading, with a high peroxidase-activity FeCN single-atom nanozyme. This platform exhibits a 7.6-fold signal enhancement over conventional chips and a detection limit of 0.03 cells mL −1 , allowing a resolvable current response from a single cell on the 2 cm 2 large-sized chip. Furthermore, it demonstrates potential feasibility for clinical detection of circulating tumor cells, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity across 55 blood samples in distinguishing cancer patients from healthy controls. This work establishes a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer paradigm and advances electrochemical cytosensing toward high-performance liquid biopsy applications.

abstract: Chemosensation underlies animal behavioral adaptation in ever-changing environments. As a member of the canonical transient receptor potential (TRP), TRPγ orchestrates the chemosensation and the adaptive behavior via fine motor control in Drosophila . Yet, how TRPγ senses and transduces chemical cues has been elusive. Here, we explore cryo-EM structures of dTRPγ in both native and camphor-bound states, with resolutions of 2.18 Å and 3.44 Å, respectively, thereby capturing ligand-induced pore dilation. Through analysis of dTRPγ channel structure, we further identify two allosteric Ca 2+ -sensing modules: an activating site embedded within the voltage-sensor-like domain (VSLD) and an inhibitory site coordinated by the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) and coiled-coil domain (CCD). These spatially segregated sensors convert cytoplasmic Ca 2+ into opposing gating signals, maintaining calcium homeostasis via a dual-feedback manner. In vivo, this bidirectional regulation directly controls locomotor kinematics by modulating stride length and velocity, while mutants with lost Ca 2+ regulatory functions exhibit impaired locomotor activity. Together, our findings reveal that dTRPγ acts as an independent ion channel, integrating environmental cues with ionic dynamics to drive adaptive behavior.

abstract: Conventional routes to strong protein fibers rely on the assembly of high-molecular-weight polymers, where mechanical performance is achieved by increasing the number of tandem repeats within the polypeptide chain. This repeat-number strategy inherently complicates production and limits scalability. Here, we introduce a contrasting paradigm in which macroscopic strength is derived not from chain length, but from the increased intrinsic mechanostability of each repeating unit. We implement this using computationally designed immunoglobulin-domain-based SuperMyo proteins, whose force-bearing β-strands are engineered to form ultra-dense hydrogen-bond networks, yielding unfolding forces nearly double those of natural immunoglobulin domains at a pulling speed of 1000 nm s −1 . When assembled into minimal tetrameric constructs (only four repeats), these designed units retain their high nanomechanical stability. Processed via wet-spinning, the tetramers form continuous macroscopic fibers with a tensile strength up to 372 MPa and a toughness of 61 MJ m⁻³. Crucially, this performance matches or exceeds that of previously reported fibers spun from polymers containing far more repeats (e.g., 64-mers). Structural analyses confirm that the enhanced stability of the monomers promotes superior β-sheet crystallization and alignment during fiber formation. By demonstrating that engineering the mechanical stability of protein building blocks is a potential strategy for producing strong protein fibers from low-repeat-number constructs, this work establishes a more efficient and scalable foundation for manufacturing high-performance protein-based materials.

title: Hippocampal replay repairs the cognitive map for flexible planning
abstract: Hippocampal replay is structured: prospective replay typically precedes retrospective replay, each aligns with the animal's future and past paths, and replay sometimes targets abandoned goals. We propose that replay repairs the cognitive map. A map that supports efficient planning precomputes expected paths; because plans terminate at the goal, the goal is part of the structure it represents. Every goal change therefore leaves the map incorrect and requires two repairs: one for the goal adopted, one for the goal left behind. The larger is expressed first, and the path each takes determines what it depicts, accounting for replay's ordering, direction, and paradoxical content. The model also generates the predictions that this ordering should invert when past and future paths converge. Recordings from rats foraging in an open arena confirm this: replay order is not as fixed as previously believed, but varies with trajectory geometry and the proximity of the abandoned goal.

title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

title: Somatostatin-excitatory coordination emerges with dexterous motor skill learning
abstract: Motor skill-learning increases spatio-temporal consistency in neuronal activity in primary motor cortex (M1), and Somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons are causally involved in these learning-related activity changes. Yet, how SST-excitatory interactions shape population level activity changes during motor skill acquisition is still unknown. Here, we imaged large populations of excitatory neurons and identified SST or parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across successive days as mice learned a dexterous, persistently M1-dependent reach-to-grasp task. Sparse, temporally coordinated, trial-resolved, and rate-controlled functional interactions between SST neurons and skill-modulated excitatory neurons emerged with learning and were stronger than those in excitatory-excitatory or PV-excitatory pairs. Interactions strengthened as neurons were recruited to the skill-modulated ensemble and weakened when skill modulation was lost. SST activity also became temporally reliable earlier than excitatory or PV activity, and SST consistency was significantly associated with behavioral performance even after controlling for training session number. Additionally, SST neurons carried more information about movement kinematics than randomly selected subsets of excitatory neurons. Overall, SST neurons became selectively coordinated with behaviorally relevant excitatory populations, revealing a cell-type-specific functional architecture for dexterous motor learning.

title: Differential endothelial cell remodeling in Down syndrome and APP duplication drives distinct blood brain barrier dysfunction
abstract: An extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene (APP) is present in Down syndrome (DS) and APP duplication (APPdup), increasing the risk of Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). However, we reported greater vascular A{beta} deposition in APPdup than in DS with AD, suggesting that other triplicated chromosome 21 genes may mitigate CAA severity. We investigated endothelial cell (EC) function and blood brain barrier (BBB) integrity in DS and APPdup using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived ECs (iECs), assessing their morphology, junctional proteins, A{beta} peptide secretion, barrier function, and transcriptomic profiles. Both DS and APPdup iECs secreted more A{beta}40 A{beta}42 compared with their respective isogenic controls but exhibited distinct A{beta} peptide profiles. DS iECs showed increased junctional protein expression and reduced permeability, whereas APPdup iECs displayed increased permeability. Transcriptomic analysis revealed extensive dysregulation in DS iECs, with enrichment of junctional, adhesion, angiogenic, immune, and apoptosis pathways, and reduced cell-cycle, proliferative, and membrane-targeting signatures. APPdup iECs showed milder changes, including impaired protein targeting and reduced adhesion-related pathways. Despite comparable APP dosage, DS iECs maintained greater junctional integrity and lower permeability than APPdup iECs, potentially contributing to differential CAA vulnerability. However, impaired proliferation and altered angiogenesis may reduce BBB resilience during ageing.

title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
abstract: Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

title: Item-specific clustering of high gamma-band activity on theta phase during speech categorization
abstract: Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a mechanism for separating neural representations in time. Although item-specific PAC has been reported, its role in perception remains unclear. Notably, previous work has shown that theta phase can bias perception, raising the question whether such biases are linked to phase-specific gamma activity. Here, we investigated whether phase-dependent perceptual biases are accompanied by item-specific theta-gamma PAC. We presented ambiguous speech sounds that could be interpreted as either /da/ or /ga/ in patients with epilepsy implanted with intracranial electrocorticography. We found that pre-stimulus theta phase predicted both the neural and perceptual response, with /da/ and /ga/ tuned channels exhibiting gamma activity clustering at distinct theta phases. These findings suggest that neural and perceptual biases stem from phase-specific pre-activation of item-specific neural representations. They demonstrate the generalizability of the theta-gamma code, shaping behavior and enhancing representational capacity.

title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. We test the hypothesis that an endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer, which is pathogenically disrupted in AD, might drive the neurodegenerative process via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling AD's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, taken together with other findings, the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

title: Generation of human iPSC-derived motor neurons with defined regional identities across the rostrocaudal axis
abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles. Together, this three-protocol pipeline enables the reproducible generation and comparative analysis of anatomically defined human motor neuron populations and provides region-matched cellular models for investigating motor neuron development, selective degeneration, and therapeutic responses.

title: Brain representations of visual short-term memories during healthy human aging: occipital decline and frontoparietal compensation
abstract: Visual short-term memory declines steeply with age, but the link to neural representations of memory content remains unknown. We used fMRI decoding to relate remembered motion-direction representations in visual and frontoparietal cortex to age and performance, in 115 adults, aged 25-87, from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) cohort. Decoding was strongest in visual cortex, but also significant in frontoparietal regions, with different profiles. Visual representations weakened with memory load and age, and statistically mediated age-related performance decline, especially during recall. This coupling, however, weakened with age: some older adults retained stronger visual representations than performance implied, suggesting impaired access to a partially preserved memory trace. Frontoparietal representations, instead, were largely insensitive to load and strengthened with age during maintenance, partially offsetting performance decline. Therefore, interventions to boost VSTM in older adults might target compensatory frontoparietal representations during memory maintenance, and readout of untapped visual representations at recall.

title: Lexical surprisal drives pupil dilation during continuous story listening
abstract: The pupil famously adjusts its dilation in response to light, but its role extends far beyond this basic sensory function. Its fluctuations index arousal and mental effort, beyond luminance-related dynamics, making it a sensitive marker of internal cognitive states. A growing body of work shows that these pupil-linked signals extend beyond the visual domain. However, which processes drive pupil responses in more naturalistic settings remains unclear as most evidence comes from tightly controlled paradigms that strip away the richness of real-world experience. Language offers a uniquely powerful window into this question, as it can allow us to create rich paradigms without having any visual, i.e. luminance, confounds. Moreover, language comprehension hinges on continuous prediction: listeners constantly generate expectations about upcoming input, and the discrepancy between expectation and actual input - contextual prediction error, or surprisal - carries measurable cognitive costs. Here, we tested the hypothesis that pupil-linked arousal indexes these linguistic surprisal signals during naturalistic listening. We recorded pupil responses while volunteers listened to naturalistic spoken stories in darkness, which were either intact or reversed. Reversed speech preserves the acoustics of the signal while destroying its intelligibility. Pupil dilation selectively tracked lexical surprisal within a late window of 1,700 to 2,350 milliseconds following word onset, in forward, but not control, backward speech. These findings indicate that pupil-linked arousal is tuned to global, context-dependent processing, tracking the cognitive cost of updating a predictive model during naturalistic listening.

title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
abstract: Increased cortical surface area of the brain's salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9-10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11-12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

title: Glutamatergic and Redox Abnormalities in Major Depressive Disorder: Links to Childhood Maltreatment and Perceived Stress
abstract: Background: Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) increases the risk for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain poorly understood. We examined (1) associations of medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) glutamatergic metabolites and redox balance with childhood maltreatment and MDD; and (2) whether these neurochemical measures predicted future perceived stress. Methods: Using proton and phosphorus 4T magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we quantified glutamate, glutamine, their sum (Glx), and the NAD/NADH ratio within the same mPFC voxel in 71 women across four groups: healthy controls (HC; n=27), current MDD without CSA (n=14), current MDD with CSA (n=14), and remitted MDD with CSA (n=16). Results: Glutamate and Glx levels were lower in both CSA-exposed groups (n=30) compared with HC (n=27), whereas women with MDD without CSA did not differ significantly from HC. Among CSA-exposed women, greater maltreatment severity was associated with lower glutamine, and greater maltreatment multiplicity with lower glutamate and Glx, specifically in women with current MDD. The association between depressive symptom severity and glutamine differed by CSA history. A significant interaction between baseline NAD/NADH ratio and clinical group predicted perceived stress at 6-month follow-up, adjusting for baseline perceived stress. Specifically, lower baseline NAD/NADH ratio predicted greater subsequent perceived stress in MDD without CSA, but not in the other clinical groups. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that mPFC glutamatergic metabolites and redox balance show distinct patterns of association with CSA history, depression status, and subsequent perceived stress, highlighting neurochemical heterogeneity in MDD and molecular markers of risk.

title: Measuring conscious tactile perception without report: pupil, blink, and microsaccade signatures of a tactile no-report paradigm
abstract: Conscious perception is often inferred from behavioral reports, which conflate awareness-related neural signals with the motor and decision processes required to respond. No-report paradigms address this by using spontaneous physiological signals, such as eye movements, to infer perception. Although our group developed a no-report visual paradigm, we had not applied this approach to touch. We developed a no-report tactile paradigm using the Galileo stimulation system to deliver pneumatic air puffs to non-thumb fingers on both hands while tracking eye movements. Participants reported sensations from the Report hand while receiving threshold-level puffs on both hands; eye metrics were used to infer perception in the No-Report hand. Perceived threshold-level stimuli elicited greater pupil dilation and more post-stimulus blinking than identical unperceived stimuli, with effects lasting 1 - 2 seconds. Microsaccade rate decreased after stimulus onset, but this suppression did not reach statistical significance. A stacked support vector machine trained on the Report eye-tracking measures was applied to classify No-Report trials and successfully separated [Predicted] Perceived from [Predicted] Not Perceived trials (AUC = .92; cross-validated accuracy = 72%; sensitivity = 90% at 80% specificity; label-permutation p < .001). These findings show that eye tracking can detect conscious tactile perception without overt responses and offer a noninvasive, scalable approach for studying tactile perception in patients with self-reported disabilities, including comatose or intubated patients.

title: Theta-Phase Targeted Encoding Gates Memory Sensitivity
abstract: Theta phase has been proposed to play an important role in memory. It may gate encoding and retrieval, such that certain phases are more favorable for memory processing than others, or become part of the memory representation, such that reinstating the encoding phase benefits retrieval. To test and distinguish these competing accounts, we used a closed-loop EEG system, allowing us to control the phase at which items were presented at encoding and retrieval. In an associative memory task, visual targets were presented at predefined phases of the ongoing mid-frontal theta rhythm, thereby pairing individual memory items with specific encoding phases. During retrieval, targets appeared either at the same phase as during encoding or at an alternative phase. We show that theta phase during encoding predicted subsequent memory sensitivity, while finding no evidence that retrieval phase nor the match between encoding and retrieval phases influenced performance. Therefore, our findings are consistent with a gating account, in which the rhythmic state at the moment of encoding influences the efficacy of memory formation.

title: Pregnancy History and Loss of Normal PSEN2 Function Impact Female Late-Life Cognitive Processing, Inhibitory Signaling, and Gliosis
abstract: Background. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is well-documented to be more progressive in affected females. It is thus critical to define how female-specific life experiences interact with AD-related risk factors to impact disease trajectory and functional burden. For example, pregnancy exerts dramatic influences on the maternal immune system, behavior, and neuroplasticity, specifically in hippocampal and limbic structures. The long-term clinical impacts from pregnancy history (parity) on late-life AD outcomes are, however, conflicting. Thus, we investigated the late-life functional impacts of parity on rodent cognitive function, inhibitory neuron density, and glial biology with loss of normal function of the AD-related risk factor, presenilin 2 (PSEN2). Methods. Female PSEN2 knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice with (multiparous) and without (nulliparous) pregnancy history were challenged at 10-15 months-old in the T-maze (TM) and Open Field Test (OFT), followed by immunofluorescence for neuronal signaling and gliosis markers. Results. Neither parity history nor PSEN2 deficiency impacted hippocampally-mediated spatial working memory of aged female mice in the TM. However, both PSEN2 KO and multiparous mice exhibited decreased OFT locomotor behavior. Multiparous mice also showed reduced OFT center zone exploration (p=0.0045) suggesting a more anxious phenotype. Parity history generally increased inhibitory marker expression in dorsal hippocampus (p=0.017), prefrontal cortex (p=0.021), and amygdala (p=0.035). Parity generally blunted oligodendrocyte marker expression in CA1 (p<0.05), while boosting astrocyte and microglia marker expression in CA3 of dorsal hippocampus. Conclusion. This work suggests that although parity history and PSEN2 deficiency exert individual differing age-related effects on cognition and neurobiology, they do not act synergistically.

title: Neural mechanisms for resilient sensory computation under metabolic stress
abstract: Food-restricted mice can solve visual discrimination tasks despite reduced synaptic currents and increased noise resulting from cellular changes in the primary visual cortex. Combining neural recordings and modeling, we study the population structure of the noise and show it is mainly concentrated along task-irrelevant directions in high-dimensional population activity, hence preserving coding on the low-dimensional stimulus manifold. In addition, we predict that food restriction shortens decision times, conserving energy but limiting the evidence accumulation needed for fine discrimination.

title: Comparative Proteomics Reveals Cell-Type-Specific Heterogeneity of Human Neural Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly explored as biomarkers and as drug delivery vehicles for the brain, yet how EV cargo differs among neural cell types at baseline remains poorly defined. This gap limits both the interpretation of disease-associated EV changes and the rational choice of EV source for therapeutic use. Here, we compared EVs from human neuronal-like SH-SY5Y cells (N-EV), astrocytes (AS-EV), and HMC3 microglia (MG-EV) side by side using tandem mass tag (TMT)-based quantitative proteomics, with all samples analyzed in a single multiplexed batch. EV identity was supported by TEM, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and canonical MISEV2023 markers. Size, zeta potential, and protein content per vesicle were comparable across EV types, whereas N-EV showed the highest particle concentration and protein yield. Enrichment analyses and consensus clustering showed cargo consistent with parental-cell functions: neuronal connectivity and structural remodeling in N-EV, extracellular support and cellular interaction in AS-EV, and immune surveillance in MG-EV. Cross-comparison also revealed patterns beyond these canonical roles, including complement-associated cargo shared by N-EV and MG-EV and a Glial-EV signature of chromatin-associated and epigenetic regulatory proteins shared by AS-EV and MG-EV. We further defined cell-type-specific signature proteins; interaction networks of the larger sets were consistent with the enrichment results. Overall, these data provide a baseline comparative reference of EV proteomes from human neural cell models for interpreting disease-associated alterations, selecting EV sources for therapeutic use, and generating hypotheses on selective cargo sorting.

title: Evolutionary tuning of complexin-synaptotagmin fusion clamp governs regulated neurotransmitter release
abstract: Synaptic vesicles must be held in a fusion-ready but restrained state until calcium influx triggers release. Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) and Complexin (CPX) both contribute to this fusion clamp, yet removing either protein produces opposite effects in different species. Whether this reflects genuine divergence in their molecular roles, or species-specific tuning of a conserved mechanism, has remained unresolved. Here we address this by comparing mammalian and C. elegans orthologs in a reconstituted single-vesicle assay that isolates clamping from upstream docking and priming. We find that clamping in both species requires the combined action of CPX and Syt1, with neither sufficient on its own. CPX clamps only with its cognate SNARE complex, a specificity conferred entirely by its accessory helix. The Syt1 orthologs differ markedly in intrinsic clamping strength, which maps to C2B mediated higher-order oligomerization and sets the functional dependence on CPX in each system. These results support a dual-regulator model of exocytosis in which Syt1 and CPX act sequentially and cooperatively through discrete molecular states to control vesicle clamping and calcium-triggered release. This framework reconciles long-standing functional discrepancies across species and reveals how evolutionary divergence modulates conserved mechanisms governing synaptic fidelity.

title: Rapid switching of in-phase and anti-phase interhemispheric rhythms within a single theta cycle: a mechanistic explanation
abstract: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) supports memory consolidation and spatial navigation. In vivo recordings of local field potential (LFP) from RSG reveal coexisting gamma (30-80 Hz) and spline (100-160 Hz) oscillations, coupled to distinct phases of the background theta ([~]8 Hz) rhythm. Remarkably, bilateral recordings reveal that gamma and splines exhibit divergent interhemispheric phase relationships: gamma is in-phase across hemispheres, while splines are anti-phase. Here, using numerical bifurcation analysis of next-generation neural mass models, we show that RSG oscillations within a single hemisphere can be understood as alternation of PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma) and ING (interneuron gamma) mechanisms in an excitatory-inhibitory network. Theta-frequency external drive to the inhibitory population switches the network between these two rhythms. Next, we build canonical interhemispheric circuits, composed of two such excitatory-inhibitory modules, delay-coupled across hemispheres. These circuits switch between in-phase gamma and anti-phase splines within a single theta cycle, reproducing the cross-spectral statistics of experimental RSG recordings. Finally, we present analytical results for threshold-linear neural mass models, showing cross-hemispheric phase patterning is governed by the ratio of cross-hemispheric delay to local inhibitory delay; we obtain explicit ranges of this ratio for which RSG-like patterning could be expected. Our work establishes that the unique oscillatory profile of RSG can be explained parsimoniously by minimal interhemispheric circuit configurations and provides a framework for experimental interrogation of interhemispheric rhythms.

title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

title: Representational geometry of punishment learning across basolateral amygdala neurons
abstract: Punishment learning allows animals to suppress actions that cause harm while maintaining actions that earn reward. Although the basolateral amygdala is necessary for punishment learning, how its population activity changes across learning, and how this activity reflects an action's consequences, remain unknown. We used longitudinal calcium imaging to track 1,147 basolateral amygdala neurons in male mice across instrumental training, punishment, choice test, and punishment extinction. Punishment learning transformed basolateral amygdala neuron activity associated with the punished action. This activity diverged from that associated with the unpunished action and became aligned with activity evoked by the punisher itself. This alignment was action and contingency specific. It preserved the direction of individual neurons' responses to the punisher: neurons activated by the punisher become more activated by the punished action alone, whereas neurons inhibited by the punisher become more inhibited by the punished action alone. We then asked whether reward and punishment were encoded separately or on a common value dimension across basolateral amygdala neurons. Punishment added a strong shock component to action-related activity without reducing its reward component, while reward and shock themselves occupied largely orthogonal population directions. Thus, during punishment learning, basolateral amygdala population activity can encode opposing consequences of the same action instead of simply changing what that action is worth.

title: Bridging Sensory Extraction and Decision Dynamics: Face Pareidolia Emergent from Bottom-Up and Top-Down Interactions
abstract: Face pareidolia-the illusory perception of faces in everyday objects-provides a unique window into how the human brain resolves visual ambiguity. Whether pareidolia arises from bottom-up sensory processing or top-down, expectation-driven feedback, is currently debated. Here we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants viewed rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) streams of images, each of which was an object-to-face morph generated along a 21-image continuum via text-to-image diffusion models. Time-resolved representational similarity analyses revealed a clear spatiotemporal dissociation, in which early occipitotemporal areas tracked physical feature changes linearly, while later frontocentral channels collapsed this structural gradient into a sharp, sigmoidal profile reflecting discrete categorical decisions (face-like versus object-like). To characterise information transmission between these regions, we implemented a novel transformation-based representational connectivity analysis. These analyses uncovered an initial feedforward flow of information that transferred and transformed posterior linear traces into anterior sigmoidal representations. Crucially, partitioning the image continuum revealed that unambiguous stimuli (faces or objects) were predominantly resolved via feedforward information flow, whereas ambiguous pareidolic images recruited prolonged top-down feedback. Furthermore, perceptual decision sensitivity was biased by animacy priors and directly predicted individual behavioural reaction times during the task. Together, the findings help reconcile prior debate by establishing that face pareidolia is neither a feedforward process nor an isolated top-down projection, but an active, multi-stage recurrent process driven by feedforward feature extraction and top-down categorical resolution.

title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge
abstract: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition.

title: Behavioral Markers of Essential Tremor Correlate with Distributed Alteration of Brain Functional Connectivity
abstract: Essential Tremor (ET) is a common motor disorder characterized by involuntary oscillations of the upper limbs during voluntary movement. Although increasing evidence implicates dysfunction of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, ET remains a diagnosis of exclusion, as no definitive biological marker currently exists. To better characterize ET, we recently hypothesized that impaired compensation of sensorimotor delays within the long-latency feedback pathways may generate the tremor-like oscillations observed in ET. This theory suggests that the mean spectral amplitude (MSA), derived from limb kinematics, may serve as a potential marker of ET. Here we investigated the relationship between MSA, standard clinical assessment (Fahn Tolosa Marin Tremor Rating Scale; FTM-TRS), and brain connectivity derived from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Using seed-based analyses, we replicated previous findings of reduced functional connectivity between the dentate nucleus and components of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway in ET patients compared with neurologically intact (NI) age-matched participants. Graph-theoretical analyses of whole-brain functional networks revealed distributed alterations in network topology across motor-related cortical and subcortical regions. Several graph metrics correlated with FTM-TRS scores and/or MSA, particularly within motor-related cortical and subcortical circuits, including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in ET. These findings indicate that ET is characterized by distributed alterations in functional brain networks beyond reduced connectivity of dentate nucleus and highlights MSA as a candidate quantitative marker linking altered brain connectivity to sensorimotor delay-driven tremor oscillations.

title: TMEM106B C-Terminal fragment aggregation exacerbates 	α-synuclein and TDP-43 proteinopathy phenotypes.
abstract: Genetic variation in the human gene encoding the lysosomal transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B) drives risk of neurodegenerative dementia. A C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B (TMEM CT) accumulates in lesions across neurodegenerative disease, potentially contributing to neurotoxicity and hampering efficacy of therapeutic interventions. Previously, we developed the first transgenic organism model of TMEM CT neuronal aggregation in Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans). We demonstrated that TMEM CT neuronal aggregation drives severe neuronal dysfunction and neuronal loss. To investigate the potential synergistic interaction of TMEM CT aggregation with other types of aggregated neurotoxic proteinopathies occurring in dementia, we assessed neuronal degeneration and pathogenic protein accumulation in bigenic C. elegans expressing TMEM CT and other key proteinopathies of neurodegeneration including a-synuclein, tau, and TAR DNA binding protein 43 (TDP-43). Our results showed strong neurotoxic synergy of TMEM106B with TDP-43 or -synuclein. However, we detected only mild synergy between TMEM106B and tau. This work provides evidence in support of TMEM CT aggregation as a significant participant in the neurodegenerative process attributed to other toxic protein aggregates. The work also highlights the importance of considering secondary proteinopathy contributions including TMEM CT aggregation when developing interventions against primary TDP-43 or -synuclein proteinopathies.

title: Concussive Injury in Human Forebrain Organoids Alters Neurogenesis and Neuroimmune Signaling
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of long-term neurological disability, yet the mechanisms underlying human-specific injury responses remain poorly understood. Rodent models of TBI have yielded significant insights into mechanisms and pathophysiology of TBI but may not capture human-specific developmental and molecular responses. Here, we establish a human forebrain organoid (hFBO) injury paradigm to examine developmental stage and region-specific responses to concussive injury. Dorsal and ventral hFBOs, enriched in glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, respectively, showed progressive physiological maturation with rudimentary firing characteristics at 80 days in vitro (DIV) and spontaneous synaptic activity by 150 DIV. Injury to dorsal and ventral hFBOs at 25 DIV, when neural progenitors dominate, caused cell death that scaled with severity and increased expression of neural proliferation markers and TLR4/NF-{kappa}B associated neuroimmune signaling. Injury to physiologically mature organoids at 150 DIV produced severity-dependent acute intracellular calcium dysregulation. Together, these findings establish a human organoid-based platform that captures developmental stage-dependent neurogenic, molecular, and cellular dysfunction in responses to concussive injury.

title: Defining cell type-specific diurnal gene expression in the mouse retina
abstract: The mammalian retina exhibits daily oscillations in gene expression that contribute to retinal physiology and visual function. However, the extent to which these temporal patterns differ among retinal cell types remains incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing in the mouse retina over the day and night, identifying rhythmic genes in the six major retinal cell types. Distinct diurnal gene expression patterns across photoreceptors, interneurons, retinal ganglion cells, and Muller glia correspond to their diverse functions across the light cycle. Even core circadian clock genes exhibited differences in paralog expression and rhythmicity across the retina. In contrast, dopamine signaling via the DRD4 receptor is highly rhythmic across most retinal cell types, suggesting dopamine signaling may be a key rhythmicity cue in the retina under diurnal conditions. This dataset highlights the complexity of daily transcriptional regulation in the retina and provides a resource to explore cell-type-specific diurnal rhythms.

title: Alterations in phototransduction timing, dark adaptation and GNAT1 trafficking in GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis.
abstract: GNAT1 (also called -transducin) is the -subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein present in rod photoreceptors that plays a critical role in phototransduction. Photoactivated rhodopsin binds GNAT1, which stimulates phosphodiesterase to hydrolyze cGMP, closing ion channels and hyperpolarizing the rod cell. To examine the effects of GNAT1 ablation on light-induced autophagy and light-exacerbated retinal degeneration, we previously generated genetically chimeric, GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis using CRISPR technology. Here, we interbred these F0 animals to produce F1 animals with defined genotypes, including full knockouts, and characterized the F1 generation by Western blot, histology, and electroretinography (ERG). In X. laevis tadpoles with nonsense mutations in all four GNAT1 alleles, the GNAT1 protein was absent, and the scotopic ERG was absent, indicating full knockout. In animals with reduced GNAT1 expression, we observed increased A- and B-wave implicit times. Greater GNAT1 protein reduction was associated with greater ERG delay, demonstrating a role for GNAT1 in the timing of phototransduction. We also identified two unexpected phenotypes linked to distinct gene edits. The Q184L-GNAT1.L mutation conferred an ERG phenotype similar to that of a full knockout, but with minimal reduction in GNAT1 protein levels, consistent with loss of function. This mutation is also present in the human population. A three-base-pair deletion (T183,Q184[->]K183) in GNAT1.S caused dominantly inherited diminished ERG response and defective dark adaptation, and was associated with photoreceptor structural abnormalities and GNAT1 accumulation at the connecting cilium, consistent with a dominant-negative effect on GNAT1 trafficking.

title: The Parkinson's disease-associated A53E mutation decreases alpha-synuclein aggregation and phosphorylation in vivo
abstract: Abnormal -synuclein aggregation is the defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) and related synucleinopathies. Rare disease-causing alpha-synuclein mutations either accelerate or slow fibrillization in vitro, however their effects in vivo are less well understood. Interestingly, the A53E mutation slows fibrillization in vitro but causes a more virulent form of PD. We use an in vivo model to examine the aggregation dynamics of disease-causing A53E and E46K alpha-synuclein mutations. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching within presynaptic terminals shows that A53E-alpha-synuclein is significantly more mobile than E46K- or wild-type (WT)-alpha-synuclein. Longitudinal analysis in vivo reveals that E46K- and WT-alpha-synuclein become progressively less mobile over days, while A53E maintains high mobility, suggesting delayed progression toward aggregated states. We also find that A53E-alpha-synuclein lacks detectable disease-relevant phosphorylation at serine-129, unlike E46K-and WT-alpha-synuclein. To mechanistically test whether this unique lack of phosphorylation drives its high mobility, we genetically modified A53E-alpha-synuclein to mimic S129 phosphorylation, and show that this manipulation indeed decreases its mobility, directly implicating the phosphorylation status of this residue in mobility.

title: Odor representations are structured by heterogeneous tuning and concentration-dependence of functionally distinct olfactory sensory neuron subpopulations.
abstract: Olfactory stimuli (odorants) are represented by combinatorial patterns of olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) activation that are translated into spatially-organized glomerular maps at their input to the CNS. How glomerular maps relate to odorant features - including chemical structure and concentration - remains a key question in understanding the neural mechanisms of odor coding. Here, we compared glomerular response maps for the same 59 odorants across three concentration regimes, using GCaMP6 imaging from OSN axon terminals in the olfactory bulb (OB) of the anesthetized mouse. At the lowest regime, in which concentrations were chosen to distinguish the most sensitive glomeruli for each odorant, glomeruli were exceptionally narrowly tuned and responses across glomeruli were extremely sparse. We then compared responses at two higher-concentration regimes, 'low' and 'high', differing by 25-fold from each other and 2 - 5 log units higher than the 'most-sensitive' regime. Increasing concentration broadened tuning of OSN inputs; this broadening was heterogeneous across chemical space and was well-described by classifying glomeruli into several subpopulations with distinct consensus tuning profiles. Each subpopulation was selectively tuned to one or a few odorant chemical classes and spatially clustered in a manner consistent with the projection patterns of receptor-defined OSN classes. Glomerular subpopulations retained distinct tuning and spatial localization even at the highest concentrations. OSN subpopulations thus sample chemical space nonuniformly across a large concentration range. These results suggest a lower-dimensional structure in the representation of odorant information that largely reflects OSN subpopulations which, in turn, map to olfactory receptor subfamilies. This organization may enable distinct odor coding strategies for different OSN classes and for parts of chemical feature space with distinct ethological relevance.

title: Direct cortical feedforward and feedback pathways differentially shape visual responses and selectively engage looped circuits
abstract: Nearly every computational account of hierarchical cortex rests on assumptions about the influence of direct cortico-cortical inputs and which neurons they act upon. Yet, disentangling their direct functional contributions from indirect, multisynaptic influences remains difficult. We examined how feedforward (FF) and feedback (FB) pathways between mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and posteromedial cortex (PM) modulate visual responses, combining retrograde labelling, multi-area two-photon imaging and optogenetic perturbations. High or low activity in either pathway was associated with both excitation and inhibition of neurons in the targeted areas. FF activity was associated with stronger additive changes, while FB activity was related to stronger multiplicative modulations and improvements in visual decoding. Optogenetic manipulations causally confirmed these asymmetries. Both pathways preferentially modulated reciprocating "looped" neurons, with FF exciting them and FB either exciting or inhibiting them. These findings demonstrate that feedforward and feedback pathways serve distinct functional roles within recurrent cortical loops.

title: The human circular Tau 12->7 RNA is translated in mouse neurons and promotes tau aggregation
abstract: In addition to numerous mRNA isoforms, the human microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) gene generates circular RNAs that are not known to be expressed in rodents. Using adeno associated viruses, we expressed human circular Tau RNA generated from backsplicing of exon 12 to exon 7 (circTau 12->7) in mouse brain. We observed rolling circle translation of circTau 12->7, similar to cultured human HEK293 cells. Despite using a ubiquitously active promoter, circTau 12->7 protein and a control circEGFP protein were only observed in mouse neurons, indicating neuron-specific translation of these circular RNAs. CircTau 12->7 expression resulted in tau aggregates resembling neurofibrillary tangles in mouse brain that included endogenous mouse tau protein. Our data support a model where neuron-specific translation of circTau RNAs induces 'linear', mRNA-translated tau aggregation, which could contribute to tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. Thus, targeting circTau RNAs could be a therapeutic approach for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Movement refinement and cholinergic regulation of outcome-dependent updating during skilled reaching.
abstract: Motor skill learning transforms initially variable actions into precise and reproducible movements, yet conventional measures of task success can obscure the distinct processes through which this refinement occurs. We combined detailed outcome scoring and kinematic analysis of single-pellet reaching in mice to resolve how individual components of the action change with practice. Decomposing reaching into successive stages revealed improvements in targeting and retrieval, while grasp success after pellet contact did not change detectably. Paw trajectories became more consistent across both successful and unsuccessful reaches, whereas changes in the mean speed profile were detected in successful reaches. To examine how striatal cholinergic signaling contributes to movement refinement and the influence of recent outcomes on subsequent actions, we monitored acetylcholine (ACh) in vivo and inhibited cholinergic interneurons (CINs) during training. ACh was elevated before reach onset and declined during execution across all reach outcomes, with no detectable change between early and late training. CIN inhibition had little effect on movement refinement across days, but altered how recent outcomes influenced the next reach, most clearly following attempts in which the pellet was grasped and then lost. These findings distinguish refinement of the practiced movement from outcome-dependent adjustments to its execution. Together, they raise the possibility that the pre-reach ACh elevation plays a role in enabling the evaluation of recent outcomes to update the execution of the next reach.

title: Projection Neurons from Infralimbic (IL) to the Basolateral Amygdala (BLA) are Critical for the Expression of Social Familiarity induced Anxiolysis (SoFiA) in rats
abstract: Mental health is crucially linked to social behavior. Healthy social behavior involves learning to adapt emotional responses to social cues, for example learning to suppress anxiety through social familiarity, or social familiarity-induced anxiolysis (SoFiA). SoFiA is well documented and forms the basis for interpersonal therapy, however, the neural mechanisms of SoFiA are unclear. SoFiA is modeled in rats by employing the social interaction habituation (SI-hab) protocol. Using SI-hab protocol, it has been determined that SoFiA represents social safety learning, which requires both anxiogenic stimulus and social familiarity during training sessions (5-6 daily SI sessions), and SoFiA expression is dependent on infralimbic subdivision (IL) of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Here we investigated the role of IL in SoFiA acquisition and expression, using chemogenetics to inhibit IL neurons. Male Wistar rats received bilateral viral injections targeting the IL or BLA and left undisturbed for 5-7 weeks to allow for viral expression. We chemogenetically inhibited via low doses of ip. clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) either the IL, the BLA, or the projections neurons from the IL to the BLA during expression of SoFiA in rats. We found that projection neurons from IL to the BLA are critical for the recovery SI behavior from the attenuation caused by the bright light (expression of SoFiA). Furthermore, CNO inhibited IL neurons with projections to the BLA and there were no off target effects of CNO on the behavioral measures. These results suggest an essential role of the IL-BLA pathway in social safety learning.
