title: Junctional Nanodomains Organised by Extended Synaptotagmin-1 Underlie Inflammatory Signalling in Sensory Neurons
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) junctions coordinate Ca2+ signalling and nociceptor excitability during inflammation, but the molecular scaffold governing assembly of signalling complexes remains unclear. Here, we identify Extended Synaptotagmin-1 (Esyt1) as a key, dynamic regulator of inflammatory pain signalling. In nociceptive DRG neurons, Esyt1 is co-expressed with ANO1 and IP3R1. Time-resolved proximity ligation assays and super-resolution microscopy showed that bradykinin rapidly increased ANO1-Esyt1 nanoscale proximity, while IP3R1-Esyt1 interactions were dynamically reorganised during ANO1-IP3R1 complex formation. Esyt1 knockdown reduced bradykinin-evoked ANO1 activity, impaired store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE), decreased STIM1-Orai1 complex formation, and disrupted ER Ca2+ store refilling. Simultaneous imaging of Ca2+ dynamics and ANO1 activity demonstrated functional coupling between SOCE and ANO1 that required Esyt1. Furthermore, in-vivo Esyt1-knockdown significantly reduced bradykinin-induced nocifensive behaviour. Together, these findings identify Esyt1 as a Ca2+-responsive scaffold that organises ER-PM signalling nanodomains and promotes inflammatory pain signalling.

title: An energy-dependent integrate-and-fire model explains coordinated synaptic and intrinsic adaptation under metabolic stress
abstract: Neuronal computation is constrained by the energetic cost of maintaining synaptic transmission, ionic gradients and action-potential generation. Prior work has shown that food restriction in mice shifts visual cortical neurons toward a different operating regime characterized by reduced excitatory synaptic drive, increased membrane resistance and a more depolarized resting membrane potential. This preserves neuronal firing rates, but comes at the cost of reduced coding precision. Deriving an improved estimate of neuronal energy consumption, we have recently shown that these adaptations reflect an optimal trade-off between neuronal information transmission and energy consumption. However, it remains unclear through which control strategies individual neurons adapt their biophysical parameters to maintain a favorable energy-information trade-off. Here we consider several candidate models implementing different control strategies. A "synapses-first" model, in which metabolic stress drives a downscaling of synaptic efficacies to save energy, while an intrinsic plasticity mechanism increases excitability to preserve the average firing rate, successfully reproduces key experimental observations. Alternative models in which energy shortages drive changes in intrinsic excitability or firing-rate variability can also reproduce the endpoint of neuronal adaptation, but predict different time courses and exhibit less energy-efficient and less stable dynamics. New experiments are needed to distinguish among these competing models.

title: Anatomical Connectivity of the Macaque Gaze-following Patch
abstract: The macaque gaze-following patch (GFP) is a specialized region of the temporal cortex implicated in decoding others' focus of attention and guiding gaze-following behavior. Although the GFP has been characterized functionally, its anatomical connectivity remains largely unknown. To investigate how the GFP is embedded within a putative brain network supporting social interactions, we injected a pair of fluorescence labeled anterograde and retrograde tracers into the GFP of one monkey. Analysis of the resulting material revealed reciprocal connections between the GFP and a region of the inferior parietal lobule, likely corresponding to area PFG, as well as sparse retrograde labeling in the amygdala. In contrast to the expectation that the GFP might be subject to cognitive control signals from the prefrontal cortex, we failed to identify convincing retrograde labeling in prefrontal regions. Overall, this connectivity profile is consistent with a network that translates information derived from others' faces into shifts of attention, while providing little evidence for direct prefrontal control of the GFP.

title: Affective representations and brain-body dynamics during emotional video viewing
abstract: Emotional events evoke changing neural and bodily responses, but how these responses relate to overall emotional evaluations and how brain and body responses correspond over time remain unclear. Ninety-two participants viewed 25 silent emotional videos, each approximately one minute long, and rated valence and arousal after each video. We recorded brain activity using magnetoencephalography alongside cardiac, electrodermal, respiratory and facial-muscle activity. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compared source-resolved cortical spectral patterns and peripheral response patterns with participants' valence and arousal ratings, adjusting each affective dimension for the other. Across whole videos, valence similarity corresponded to beta-band power patterns predominantly in left sensorimotor and frontotemporal cortex and to facial-muscle responses. Arousal similarity corresponded to alpha-band power patterns in the right frontoparietal cortex and to phasic electrodermal activity. The neural associations persisted after adjustment for visual and semantic similarities between the videos. Windowed neural correspondence with retrospective valence was significant from around 10 s onwards, with both neural and facial-muscle associations strengthening towards the end of the videos, whereas no significant windowed arousal associations were detected throughout viewing. We further applied dynamic RSA to compare neural and physiological response patterns across videos at different temporal lags. Correspondence exceeded a temporally decoupled reference for facial muscles, heart rate and electrodermal activity, but not respiration rate. On average, corrugator activity preceded corresponding neural patterns by about 1 s, zygomaticus activity occurred at approximately the same time, and heart-rate and electrodermal activity followed about 1.7 s and 4.5 s later, respectively. Together, these findings link overall affective evaluations to complementary neural and peripheral response geometries and reveal signal-specific temporal profiles of ongoing brain-body correspondence.

title: A preclinical platform for focused ultrasound delivery from microplate to awake brain
abstract: Background. Focused ultrasound (FUS) has broad therapeutic potential, but its mechanisms of action are poorly understood. Preclinical FUS research enables rigorous interrogation of understudied parameters, but fragmented, single-purpose benchtop devices prevent standardized acoustic exposure across models. Objective. To describe a unified preclinical FUS platform for cell culture, ex vivo tissue, and awake stereotaxic in vivo delivery in one lightweight system, validated using glioblastoma as a disease model. Methods. We performed single-well FUS delivery to 96-well microplates, single-well delivery to freshly resected human glioblastoma tissue, and stereotaxic transcranial delivery to awake, head-fixed mice ambulating freely on a floating cage. Output was independently calibrated in free field, with measured microplate insertion loss. Pulsed low-intensity focused ultrasound (pLIFU) was applied to GL261-bearing mice, resected human glioblastoma, and macrophage cell lines. Results. Awake stereotaxic pLIFU produced acute tumor signal attenuation in GL261-bearing mice (mean log2 fold-change -1.66 versus +5.20 controls, p = 0.016) with bioluminescence evidence consistent with focal targeting. Ex vivo pLIFU produced directionally consistent immunophenotypic shifts in human glioblastoma (increased iNOS+, decreased Arg1+ populations). In vitro, pLIFU reduced CD80 on immunosuppressive macrophages to 73% of baseline in RAW 264.7 cells (p = 0.0008, n = 5) and 64% in THP-1 cells (p = 0.0006, n = 2), with MHC II upregulation in RAW 264.7 (ratio 1.65, p = 0.004) and ARG1 reduction in THP-1 (ratio 0.52, p = 0.0025). Conclusions. A unified preclinical FUS platform validated across in vitro, ex vivo, and awake in vivo applications enables stereotaxically guided transcranial FUS in awake, head-fixed mice ambulating in an exploratory manner during sonication, and single-well microplate treatments.

title: Individualized brain-body signatures of positive emotions revealed by large-scale multimodal neurophysiological recording
abstract: Using one of the most comprehensive multimodal biosensing datasets in affective research, densely sampled within individuals, we asked how emotions are instantiated in each person's brain and body. Four participants viewed 168 emotion-evoking videos during 128-channel EEG and 28 autonomic, ocular and facial recordings. Cross-validated elastic-net classifiers distinguished each of 15 positive and neutral emotions from baseline in every participant (mean accuracy 87-97%). We found that no emotion was predicted by a single marker and each reflected a multimodal ensemble of cortical and autonomic activity whose composition was largely person-specific. Yet physiology-derived groupings converged selectively with self-report; Interest-Awe-Amusement-Satisfaction and Entrancement-Aesthetic Appreciation recurred across individuals based on physiology. Across emotion groups, frontal and posterior delta, posterior alpha and electrodermal activity formed a shared backbone, plausibly reflecting affective and sensory engagement, whereas cardiovascular and facial signals varied between people. This framework yields individualized, objective neurophysiological indicators of emotion, potentially aiding personalized diagnosis.

title: Executive and language systems competitively shape predictive processing during reading
abstract: When we read, our brains constantly generate predictions about upcoming words, which is thought to make comprehension faster and more efficient. Yet it remains unclear whether this predictive mechanism relies on the same domain-general executive resources the brain uses for other demanding cognitive tasks, or operates largely independently within the language system. Here we tested this question using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in twenty-five healthy adults, who performed self-paced naturalistic reading, an n-back task, and a dual task of concurrent reading and n-back, allowing us to place competing demands on cognitive resources. In three sessions, we stimulated the left angular gyrus alone, the angular gyrus together with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a hub of executive control, or delivered sham stimulation, and used computational modeling of decision-making to isolate how each brain state altered the underlying cognitive processes. Combined stimulation of the angular gyrus and prefrontal cortex selectively weakened the reading-time costs of unexpected words, but only when reading competed with the working-memory task, revealing that linguistic prediction draws on executive resources specifically under cognitive load. Computational models showed that the relationship was bidirectional: Unpredictable words also disrupted concurrent working-memory decisions, slowing the accumulation of evidence and increasing response caution. Together, these findings show that predictive language processing is not a fixed, encapsulated function but is dynamically coupled to executive control when cognitive demands compete. Our results provide evidence that prediction during language comprehension is embedded within a broader, demand-sensitive cognitive architecture that flexibly coordinates linguistic and executive resources.

title: Beyond Neural Noise: Critical Dynamics Predict Slower Reaction Times in Adults With and Without ADHD
abstract: Historically, neural variability observed during task was interpreted as noise, assumed to obscure meaningful signal and thus something to be minimized both analytically by researchers and functionally by the brain. Changes to this signal-to-noise ratio have been proposed as a possible neural mechanism behind the increased reaction-time variability (RTV) in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, not all variability is the same - in some cases, variability can have some underlying statistical structure that can be beneficial to information processing. The challenge lies in distinguishing meaningful variability from random noise. The edge-of-synchrony critical point, which describes a system poised between synchronous and asynchronous regimes, could be a good theoretical framework to study these different types of neural variability. In this study, we investigate whether changes in criticality and oscillatory dynamics preceded slower behavioral responses during a bimodal continuous performance task in ADHD. We find evidence that, prior to slower responses, neural dynamics shift toward criticality in both ADHD and control groups, suggesting that increase variability in ADHD and during attention lapses are related to structured variability and not necessarily random noise. Notably, these findings run counter predictions based on the proposed model and previous literature on neural noise in this population, challenging predictions of edge-of-synchrony criticality as a unifying account of neural variability and behavioral performance. Furthermore, this effect did not emerge at the between-subject level, underscoring the limitations of relying on between-subject correlations to infer neural mechanisms.

title: Transcranial electrical stimulation for memory enhancement: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques have received increasing interest for their potential to enhance memory function, a fundamental cognitive aspect of daily life. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the efficacy of transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) in enhancing memory function in healthy adults, following the pre-registered strategy at PROSPERO (CRD42022353630). A total of 113 articles (193 trials, 7,299 participants) examining tES were identified. Meta- analysis revealed a significant overall effect of tES on memory function compared with sham stimulation (standardised mean difference [95% confidence interval] = 0.19 [0.12, 0.25]). A positive pooled effect was also observed in the subgroup receiving frontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Stimulation was associated with positive pooled effects for working- and declarative-memory task performance. Significant pooled effects were observed within 1 day after stimulation; longer-term estimates were imprecise. Regarding adverse events, tingling and itching sensations on the scalp occurred more frequently in the active group than in the sham group, but no serious adverse events were reported. Limitations, including small- study effects, heterogeneity, and uneven coverage of memory domains, were noted, emphasising the need for improved experimental rigour and diversification of memory tasks. These findings suggest that tES is associated with small improvements in memory-task performance and was generally well tolerated under the studied protocols. Heterogeneity, small- study effects, and limited adverse-event reporting constrain conclusions about efficacy, durability, and safety

title: Sex differences in latent inhibition and their implications for psychotic disorders
abstract: Latent inhibition (LI) refers to the reduced ability to learn or express learning about a stimulus following prior exposure to it without consequence. It has been extensively studied to investigate associative learning and memory as well as the aberrant attribution of salience to irrelevant stimuli in both humans and animals, a process which is thought to underpin hallucinations and delusions in psychosis. Despite sex differences observed in numerous aspects of psychosis, few studies have attempted to characterise sex differences in LI. This systematic review outlines the current evidence of sex differences in LI in both human and rodent studies, showing predominantly inconclusive and conflicting evidence for sex differences. However, the majority of cases in which sex differences were found were in studies that assessed the impact of additional factors on LI such as drug administration, juvenile handling, and oestrous phase, and demonstrated interactions between sex and these additional factors. Hence, there is stronger evidence for sex differences in vulnerability to perturbations in LI. Furthermore, we present data demonstrating sex differences in latent inhibition of contextual fear conditioning and associated gene expression in the hippocampus in rodents, suggesting sex differences in hippocampal processing underpinning latent inhibition at both the behavioural and neurobiological levels. Although there have been relatively few studies demonstrating sex differences in LI identified by the systematic review, the data suggest that in hippocampally dependent forms of LI, sex differences may be more apparent, which may be of relevance in relation to sex differences in the presentation of psychosis.

title: Repetitive Levodopa Treatment Drives Cell Type-Specific Striatal Adaptations Associated With Progressive Dyskinesia in Parkinsonian Mice
abstract: The use of levodopa to manage Parkinsons disease (PD) symptoms leads to levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) and other motor fluctuations, which worsen with disease progression and repeated treatment. Aberrant activity of striatal D1- and D2-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-/D2-MSNs) underlies LID, but the mechanisms driving its progression remain unclear. Using the 6-OHDA mouse model of PD/LID, we combined in vivo and ex vivo recordings to isolate the effect of repeated treatment in LID worsening and other changes in the motor response to levodopa. We found that LID worsening is linked to potentiation of levodopa-evoked responses in both D1-/D2-MSNs, independent of changes in dopamine release or MSN intrinsic excitability. Instead, strengthening of glutamatergic synapses onto D1-MSNs emerged as a key signature. Moreover, we found changes in D2-MSN activity are associated with LID duration, which paralleled a reduction in D2R sensitivity. These findings reveal striatal adaptations contributing to worsening of levodopa-related complications.

title: A Complex Containing the Na+/K+ ATPase Regulates Epileptogenesis in Drosophila melanogaster
abstract: Epileptogenesis, the process through which the brain becomes seizure-prone, is not well understood. Previous work identified a novel gene in Drosophila, julius seizure (jus), that when mutated or developmentally knocked down, leads to epilepsy in adult Drosophila, providing a useful model for dissecting epileptogenesis. Here we report that when a GFP-tagged Jus was used as bait in a co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assay, a complex of 23 associated proteins was identified that included ATPalpha and Nervana 3, two subunits of the Na+/K+ ATPase. RNAi-mediated knockdown of ATPalpha, Nervana 3, or any of 8 additional complex proteins enhanced seizure susceptibility of jus mutants. The critical period for Jus expression to protect against epileptogenesis was further defined, occurring between pupal stages P4-7; remarkably, the jus seizure phenotype could be rescued by increasing neural activity of jus-expressing neurons during these mid-pupal stages, suggesting that altered neural activity in these neurons may contribute to the seizure phenotype. Our data support a model that, in wild type flies, a protein complex containing Na+/K+ ATPase and Jus prevents epileptogenesis, possibly by regulating neural activity.

title: Season-long head acceleration exposure, prior contact-sport history, and cognitive performance in British amateur American football players
abstract: Background: Head acceleration events (HAEs) are common in contact sports, but season-long exposure and its relationship with cognitive performance in amateur British American football remain poorly characterised. Methods: Thirty male players were recruited from three British amateur American football teams. Selected Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (SCAT6) components and computerised tasks were assessed across the season. Seasonal analyses included 20 participants, and exposure-linked analyses included 17. Helmet-sensor events were attributed to participants and restricted to participant-assignment and baseline-to-post-season calendar windows. Mixed-effects models assessed seasonal outcomes. Principal component analysis (PCA) summarised standardised baseline-to-post-season changes, and six exposure associations were evaluated. Results: Players recorded a mean of 768 (SD 482) events. Several individual tests improved across the season. The first principal component (PC1) explained 21.9% of change variance and had loadings with opposing signs. Prior seasons had a nominal association with PC1 (slope -0.153, 95% CI -0.305 to -0.00018; r2=0.233; p=0.0498), which did not survive six-test Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) adjustment (p=0.299). No in-season exposure association survived adjustment. Conclusion: Repeated-test performance improved, while exposure associations remained uncertain. The mixed PC1 pattern cannot be interpreted as a uniform measure of global cognitive worsening or improvement.

title: Alpha-Synuclein Co-Pathology and Amyloid-Tau Coupling in Alzheimer's Disease: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Analyses Across Braak Stage Regions
abstract: **Background:** Misfolded alpha-synuclein (alphaSyn), a common co-pathology in Alzheimer's disease, acts synergistically with amyloid and tau in animal models, but its role in the human amyloid-tau-cognition cascade is unclear. We examined whether alphaSyn modifies the amyloid-tau and tau-cognition associations, cross-sectionally and over time. **Methods:** We analyzed 615 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative with a cerebrospinal fluid alphaSyn seed amplification assay (SAA), flortaucipir tau positron emission tomography (PET) in Braak stage regions, and amyloid PET and domain-specific cognitive composites within 1 year of tau PET. Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors tested alphaSyn x amyloid interactions on regional tau and alphaSyn x tau interactions on cognition; mixed-effects models tested the same interactions on repeated tau PET (n = 341) and cognitive testing (n = 516). **Results:** alphaSyn positivity was present in 117 participants (19.0%). Cross-sectionally, the amyloid-tau association was steeper in alphaSyn SAA+ participants for meta-temporal tau (interaction beta 0.258, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.493; p = 0.032) and Braak I-IV (p <= 0.048); no interaction survived false discovery rate correction (q = 0.072), and clinical-stage adjustment attenuated it (beta 0.114; p = 0.333). Over a median of 3.5 years (n = 341; 68 alphaSyn-positive), no alphaSyn x amyloid x time interaction was detected (meta-temporal beta -0.012, 95% CI -0.046 to 0.023; p = 0.513). No cross-sectional alphaSyn x tau interaction on cognition was detected; at mean tau, alphaSyn positivity was associated with lower executive function (q = 0.032). Longitudinally, tau-related executive decline was less steep in alphaSyn-positive participants (q = 0.042). **Conclusions:** The alphaSyn-associated amyloid-tau interaction was modest, did not withstand multiple-testing correction, and had no detected longitudinal counterpart. alphaSyn positivity was associated with poorer executive function at mean tau; the unexpected longitudinal executive interaction needs replication. These findings do not establish alphaSyn status as a marker for tau-progression enrichment in trials.

title: Distinct representations of an anxiogenic environment in different cell types of the ventral hippocampus
abstract: In addition to its role in episodic memory and spatial navigation, the hippocampus has also been found to influence mood-related disorders such as anxiety and depression. These seemingly distinct roles are consistent with a functional dissociation between the two anatomical poles of the hippocampus: whereas the dorsal portion of the hippocampus in rodents is necessary for spatial tasks, the ventral portion controls affective behaviors. We have recently found that neurons in the ventral, but not dorsal, CA1 area of mice encode anxiety-related information (i.e. are "anxiety cells") in diverse defensive and exploratory behaviors. Still it is unclear how general threat-related information is computed within the hippocampal circuit. In this work, we have examined how distinct hippocampal subregions and cell types encode anxiety-related information by imaging calcium activity in large populations of genetically-defined neurons in the ventral hippocampus while mice explore the elevated plus maze (EPM), a conflict-based anxiety test. We compared the neural encoding of task-related features within the ventral CA1 (vCA1) and ventral dentate gyrus (vDG) regions in order to examine the emergence of anxiety-related activity through the hippocampal circuit. We found that granule cells (vGCs) of the vDG represented similar valence information to neurons in vCA1 in the form of arm-type specific encoding in the EPM, which suggests that encoding of anxiety-related features is already present at this first stage of hippocampal processing. When compared with ventral granule cells (vGCs), ventral mossy cells (vMCs) underlying the DG had stronger spatial encoding and less valence encoding, suggesting that they may be more functionally connected with the highly spatially sensitive dorsal hippocampus. Together these findings will help to understand the encoding of anxiety-related information in the hippocampus and how it relates to neural circuit defects in mood-related disorders.

title: NeuroMark-SZ: A Holistic Resting-State-fMRI-Based Model for Divergent Functional Circuitry in Schizophrenia
abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is a severe neuropsychiatric disorder. Efforts to describe the underlying biology and establish diagnostic markers through non-invasive neuroimaging methods are ongoing, resulting in a range of theoretical brain-based frameworks. Prominent frameworks for aberrant schizophrenia-associated functional connectivity in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) include the dysconnectivity hypothesis, theory of cognitive dysmetria, and triple network theory. Although informative, prior work can be improved by increasing sample size, avoiding confirmation bias, and accounting for individual variability and the effects of medication and chronicity. Methods: With these recommendations in mind, we employed a data-driven, whole-brain approach using a large multi-site rsfMRI dataset (N = 2,656; schizophrenia = 1,248). We used reference-guided independent component analysis to generate subject-specific whole-brain functional network connectivity (FNC) and extract imaging markers of similarity to schizophrenia patterns. We modeled the relationship between medication dosage, age of onset, chronicity, symptom severity, and cognitive performance and FNC. Results: Our analysis identified a reliable schizophrenia-FNC signature characterized by aberrantly stronger negative cerebellothalamic and positive thalamocortical connectivity, implicating sensory, motor, and associative cortical circuits. While medication and chronicity were significantly associated with these signatures, the core cerebellothalamic disruptions remained a robust marker of schizophrenia. Conclusions: This work represents the largest schizophrenia-specific rsfMRI study to date, refines existing theoretical frameworks with a more nuanced map of how clinical variables interact with brain connectivity, and provides a high-fidelity template of schizophrenia-related connectivity. We have released this template as an open-access resource to facilitate reproducibility and accelerate the development of reliable rsfMRI-based schizophrenia biomarkers.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
abstract: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
abstract: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.

title: Morphological Features of Murine Pulmonary Arterial Networks for Diagnosing Vascular Disease
abstract: Hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension results from prolonged time spent in a low-oxygen environment. The induced pulmonary hypertension leads to vascular remodeling, including vessel dilation and decreased compliance. This study aims to identify changes in vascular morphology in mice with pulmonary hypertension induced by hypoxia. To do so, we examine the pulmonary arterial network morphology using methods from geometry, topological data analysis, and statistical shape analysis. Tools from these fields are applied to arterial networks excised from micro-CT images of thirteen mice at four pressures. Networks from the hypertensive mice were normalized via a radius pruning algorithm, and analysis was conducted on the entire arterial network, as well as on a per-lobe basis. The main objective of this study was to present an adaptable pipeline for extracting features from micro-CT images to study how vascular disease affects arterial network morphology. Using this pipeline, we showed that the hypertensive mice have increased radius ratios and decreased length-to-radius ratios. Persistent homology analysis revealed that hypertension leads to lower branch-to-branch proximity and lower directional complexity in both the posterior and anterior directions. Persistence curves, particularly Betti curves, revealed lobe-specific differences in the left and inferior lobes. The first two shape principal component scores were also able to discriminate between control and hypertension at lower pressures. Importance metrics for each feature are computed using a boosted decision tree, and then an SVM classification model is fit with the most informative predictors for hypertensive classification.

title: AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
abstract: Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.

title: A heterogenetic theory of living systems
abstract: The problem of the dynamics of living systems and their mathematical representation essentially unfolds on two levels. Firstly, the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure describe how a living system produces and maintains itself. Secondly, living phenomena are recognised as historical, involving the evolution of dynamics and spaces of possibility that change over time. Currently, no differential model can incorporate both of these aspects. We propose adopting the differential heterogenesis framework, which enables us to define differential operators that change in space and time, producing event-based and historical dynamics. In this construction, heterogeneous operator assemblages will be constrained by the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure, providing a theoretical framework for event-based and historical living systems. Finally, we provide a specific example of assembly with Gray-Scott kinetic equations, along with numerical simulations and results.

title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

title: Yoga biomechanics through energy optimization: diverse kinematics and low-dimensional kinetics
abstract: Yoga is widely practiced for improving physical and mental health, yet the biomechanical demands of individual yoga poses remain poorly characterized. Existing experimental studies typically examine only a small number of poses or muscles, limiting their ability to guide pose selection for rehabilitation or exercise prescription. Here we present a computational framework for predicting whole-body joint torques and contact forces from two-dimensional images of yoga poses. The framework combines manual pose digitization, a sagittal-plane MuJoCo human model, and constrained metabolic energy minimization subject to static equilibrium. We applied the framework to 55 sagittally symmetric yoga poses from Light on Yoga, generating a dataset of joint kinematics, contact locations, and predicted joint torques and contact forces. These poses collectively span nearly the full physiological range of motion of the major joints while exhibiting a wide range of predicted joint torques, with the greatest average demands on the lower extremities and lumbar region. Principal component analysis revealed a striking contrast between kinematics and kinetics: nearly all ten dimensions were required to represent the joint-angle data, whereas the first three principal components captured over 90% of the variance in joint torques. Thus, yoga poses exhibit substantial diversity in body configurations but comparatively low-dimensional patterns of predicted joint loading. Predicted joint torque rankings were also largely insensitive to uncertainty in the relative weighting of joint metabolic costs. This framework enables systematic biomechanical analysis of yoga poses and provides a foundation for quantitatively evaluating their mechanical demands and informing future rehabilitation strategies.

title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.
comment: 18 pages main text plus 40 pages Supplementary Information

title: PCR-ALERA: A PCR-ELISA analogue but antibody-free DNA detection system
abstract: PCR-ALERA is a new concept for DNA detection that combines DNA amplification by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with an activator-linked enzyme reactivation assay (ALERA). PCR-ALERA resembles the commercial, semi-quantitative PCR-ELISA assay that offers high sensitivity and high-throughput screening in microplates. PCR-ALERA overcomes a major drawback of PCR-ELISA since it does not require the time-consuming handling of expensive antibodies. In the first step of the assay, commercially available modified nucleotides were incorporated during PCR amplification of the target DNA. A selenocysteine containing peptide (the activator) was linked to the amplified DNA by click chemistry. This peptide has been optimized for the highly efficient activation of the latent protease papain by selenolate-triggered disulfide cleavage. The DNA-peptide hybrid was then immoblized in microplate wells and incubated with latent papain. The latter was readily activated and converted a fluorogenic substrate to a fluorescent product with high catalytic turnover. Overall assay time is about 4 hours including PCR.

title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
abstract: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $χ^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

title: The Verification Wall in Microbial Metabolomics
abstract: Computational methods now propose structures for gut microbial metabolites faster than any laboratory can confirm them. We argue that verification, not generation, is the binding constraint, and that better models will not relieve it. Confirming a structure to the field's own standard means having the molecule in hand. Automation can lower what that costs per compound, but the cost stays proportional to the number of structures and never amortizes across them. Two substitutes are on offer and neither removes that requirement. In-silico spectral prediction ranks candidates instead of confirming one, and the strongest current model puts the right structure first 33.5% of the time on a scaffold-split benchmark. Any assignment resting on spectral similarity is, by the field's own definition, made without a reference standard. Microcrystal diffraction does return a structure, but it needs the compound to crystallize out of a trace mixture, which is a different problem rather than an easier one. We sorted 10,645 computationally inferred metabolite structures by what verifying each would take. Between 5% and 37% have no verification route identified under our analysis. That spread reflects where the thresholds are set rather than a measured count of unverifiable compounds, and the inaccessible ones cluster among the most speculative entries. Those figures understate the problem, because the gut makes far more compounds than any database records. HMDB holds only what someone has already thought worth cataloguing, and structure generators are bounded by nothing at all. The claim is easy to disprove. Show a route that confirms structures as fast as they are proposed. Until someone does, two problems stay unsolved. Nobody knows how to spend a verification budget that will always be too small, or what a biologist may conclude from a structure that was never confirmed.
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the AI for Science workshop (NeurIPS 2026). Code and data at https://github.com/tkoyama-keio/verification-wall-metabolomics

title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift
abstract: Video-based gait assessment often keeps only high-confidence pose observations, which can lower measurement error but change the movement assessed. We compared confidence selection with budget-matched random selection in a Parkinson-related cohort (n = 96) and an NF2-related replication cohort (n = 18). In the Parkinson-related cohort, confidence selection produced a small but consistent shift in the observed movement summary (+0.05 SD, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07), while held-out Mini-BESTest error stayed flat (-0.04 points, -0.13 to 0.05); a policy preserving motion-group proportions reduced the shift, while NF2 showed no shift and its predictor did not beat a constant baseline. Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort's window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Unchanged clinical error from such small-cohort predictors therefore cannot show that quality filtering preserves the assessed movement.

abstract: Deciphering processes that are responsible for differences in brain development and architecture among species may provide clues to the species-specific program and may facilitate a mechanistic understanding of vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders. It has recently been shown that the promoter of the CBLN2 gene, which codes for a synaptogenic factor, cerebellin 2 (Cbln2), has a repressor element in mice but not in humans. A humanized mouse lacking this repressor (hCbln2) reproduces higher spine density in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) neurons and higher corticothalamic connectivity observed in humans. Cbln2 is part of a trans-synaptic complex that includes glutamate delta-1 receptor (GluD1) and neurexins (Nrxn) (GluD1-Cbln2-Nrxn). Interestingly, we have previously reported a contrasting striatal patch-matrix expression pattern of GluD1 in mouse versus monkey, suggesting a potential role of the GluD1-Cbln complex in species differences. In this study, we examined the synaptic organization and function in the cortex and dorsal striatum of hCbln2 mice. Consistent with previous reports, hCbln2 mice exhibited increased vGluT1 expression in the mPFC, indicating enhanced intracortical connectivity. Electrophysiological recordings further revealed an increased mEPSC frequency along with a reduced mIPSC frequency in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, suggesting an increase in excitatory/inhibitory balance. These changes were accompanied by enhanced mTOR signalling and autophagic deficits in the mPFC. Contrasting synaptic changes were observed in the striatum with an increase in vGluT2 and a reduction in vGluT1, together with a decrease in GluD1-Cbln1 and an increase in hevin. Importantly, corticostriatal dysfunction characterized by a reduction in cortical contribution to mEPSCs and impaired DHPG-induced synaptic depression was observed in the hCbln2 medium spiny neurons. Further, hCbln2 mice displayed increased repetitive behaviour together with social and affective-like deficits, consistent with autism-relevant phenotypes. Collectively, these findings identify humanized Cbln2 regulation as a driver of divergent cortical and striatal synaptic remodelling, disrupted corticostriatal synaptic function, and behavioural abnormalities relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders.

abstract: Vascular and neurodegenerative pathologies frequently co-occur in aging brains, yet the mechanisms linking vascular neuropathologies to cognitive impairment remain incompletely understood. We examined whether Alzheimer's disease neuropathologic change (ADNC) and Lewy body disease (LBD) mediate or modify associations between vascular neuropathologies and domain-specific cognitive performance. The analytic sample included 1,269 decedents (mean age at death, 84.3 ± 9.1 years; 43.3% female; 94.7% White). At the last evaluation prior to death, 22.5% were cognitively normal, 2.4% were impaired but not mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 14.9% had MCI, and 60.2% had dementia. Vascular neuropathologies included arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis of the circle of Willis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), gross infarcts/lacunes, and microinfarcts. Multivariable linear regression models evaluated associations with harmonized memory, executive function, and language z-scores adjusting for age at death, sex, education, and apolipoprotein E ε4 status. Effect modification by ADNC and LBD was tested. Mediation models estimated indirect and direct effects of vascular neuropathologies on cognition through ADNC or LBD using 5,000 bootstrap samples. Greater arteriolosclerosis severity was associated with worse memory (β=-0.16, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.09), executive function (β=-0.18, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.11), and language (β=-0.18, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.12; all p<0.001). CAA was strongly associated with poorer cognition across domains, including memory (β=-0.26, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.19; p<0.001). Atherosclerosis and infarcts showed more limited associations, while microinfarcts were not significantly associated with cognition. Mediation analyses indicated that ADNC statistically accounted for approximately 13-29% of the associations between arteriolosclerosis and cognition across domains and 64-91% of the associations between CAA and cognition. Direct effects of arteriolosclerosis remained significant, whereas CAA effects were largely explained by ADNC. Effect modification by ADNC and LBD was limited, although LBD attenuated associations of arteriolosclerosis and CAA with executive function. Mediation through LBD was not observed. This novel evidence shows that vascular neuropathologies influence cognition through defined pathways with statistically significant patterns of associations. In this autopsy-confirmed cohort, vascular neuropathologies showed different patterns of association with domain-specific cognitive performance and ADNC. A larger proportion of the association involving CAA was statistically accounted for by ADNC, whereas direct associations remained more apparent for arteriolosclerosis. This study clarifies how vascular and neurodegenerative processes interact to shape cognitive impact and inform mechanistic preventions.

abstract: Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals' ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants' structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

abstract: Protein homeostasis is essential for the maintenance of peripheral axons and depends on co-ordinated protein synthesis, folding, ubiquitination and directing protein fate across multiple protein quality-control pathways. E3 ubiquitin ligases are central to this network by conferring substrate specificity and enabling precise spatiotemporal regulation of protein homeostasis. Increasing genetic and functional evidence implicates the disruption of E3 ligase function in inherited peripheral neuropathies, providing a mechanistic link between impaired proteostasis and progressive axonal degeneration. Here, we examine inherited peripheral neuropathies associated with dysfunction of Tripartite Motif-Containing Protein 2 (TRIM2), Leucine Rich Repeat and Sterile Alpha Motif Containing 1 (LRSAM1), Ubiquitin Protein Ligase E3C (UBE3C) and the Cullin-Ring 3 (CUL3) substrate adapter, Gigaxonin (GAN). Although these proteins differ in structure, substrates and disease mechanisms, their dysfunction converges on disruption of proteasomal degradation, autophagy and cytoskeletal homeostasis. By integrating these genetically distinct neuropathies within a common mechanistic framework, we propose this positions E3 ubiquitin ligases as selective regulators of multiple protein quality-control pathways and highlights the specific vulnerability of long peripheral axons to the disruption of ubiquitin-mediated proteostasis.

abstract: Pain intensity fluctuates across the day in patients, yet the cellular clock mechanisms that generate pain rhythmicity and their therapeutic potential remain poorly defined. Prior studies have established circadian variation in nociception and a requirement for intact clock function, but it has remained unclear the neurophysiological mechanisms which translate clock state into time-of-day changes in pain. The goal of this study was to define the clock component(s) and effector pathway(s) that drive pain rhythmicity and to test whether this axis can be exploited for analgesia. We combined behavioural analyses under circadian conditions with genetic dissection of clock components in sensory neurons, electrophysiological interrogation of nociceptor excitability, and pharmacological modulation of the clock machinery. To establish translational relevance, we used human iPSC-derived nociceptors, including a human pain disease model, to test whether the same clock-excitability coupling operates in human cells. We show that nociceptive behaviours exhibit robust circadian rhythmicity and that this rhythmicity depends on the molecular clock within peripheral sensory neurons. Loss of cryptochromes CRY1/CRY2 disrupts time-of-day differences in nociceptor excitability, identifying cryptochromes as essential clock effectors in the pain pathway. Mechanistically, cryptochrome state controls voltage-gated sodium channel function, providing a direct link from clock machinery to nociceptor responsiveness. Pharmacological stabilisation of cryptochromes using a small-molecule modulator suppresses sodium currents and reduces nociceptive responses across distinct pain paradigms, and this effect is abrogated when cryptochrome function is absent. In synchronised human iPSC-derived nociceptors, we observe concordant clock-state-dependent changes in excitability, and cryptochrome stabilisation reduces hyperexcitability. These findings identify a peripheral sensory neuron clock mechanism that drives pain rhythmicity through cryptochrome-dependent control of sodium channel function and highlight cryptochrome stabilisation as a non-opioid therapeutic strategy for pain disorders with diurnal symptom variation.

abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway-mediated chronic inflammation drives neurodegeneration in natural aging and various neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here, we identify Otubain-2 (OTUB2) as a pivotal regulator that orchestrates the STING signalosome to amplify inflammatory responses. The function of OTUB2 in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration was investigated through genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 in hTARDBP transgenic mice​, adeno-associated virus-mediated TDP43 overexpression mice, and aged mice. Biochemical assays were performed to dissect underlying molecular mechanisms. OTUB2 inhibited K63 ubiquitination of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), thereby suppressing TBK1 kinase activity and promoting cell death mediated by hyperactivated receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1). Additionally, OTUB2 functioned as a scaffold facilitating assembly of the TBK1-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signalling complex, a prerequisite for IRF3 phosphorylation, and enhanced IRF3 dimerization by reducing its K11 ubiquitination. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 significantly ameliorated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in both ALS and aged mouse models. This study establishes OTUB2 as a critical regulator of cGAS-STING signalling and a potential therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.

abstract: The amygdaloid complex is one of the most structurally and functionally heterogeneous regions of the mammalian brain, acting as an integrative node between sensory, mnemonic and visceral systems. It comprises a set of subnuclei whose cytoarchitectural differentiation, neurochemical profiles and anatomical boundaries have been debated since the earliest descriptions. This heterogeneity is established during ontogenetic development, assembling progenitors from pallial and subpallial domains, and preoptic and hypothalamic territories, resulting in a highly connected network. Maturation is not complete at birth, the amygdala changes through childhood and adolescence, leaving a protracted window of environmental sensitivity. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have added a molecular layer to this framework, resolving populations that no single marker separates, and set explicit limits on the resolution at which rodent-derived subdivisions can be transferred to the human amygdala. Together these levels of description provide a structural framework for understanding its functions, which include emotional regulation and conditioned fear, social and sexual behaviours, decision-making, reward and punishment processing, empathy and memory modulation. Cross-species comparison reveals further variation, particularly the expansion of the basolateral complex in primates and the redistribution of neurons towards the lateral nucleus in humans. In summary, the amygdala acts as a densely connected hub with a broad role not only in physiological and psychological health but also in disease states; indeed, the amygdala is affected early in several neurodegenerative disorders, and in some (notably limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy and argyrophilic grain disease) it is among the first regions in which pathology is detected.

abstract: Animal pollinators underpin biodiversity and global agriculture, yet the molecular mechanisms that coordinate floral rewards and signals to attract pollinators remain poorly understood. Through phenotyping melon genetic diversity, we identified nectarless1 (nls1), encoding the YABBY-family transcription factor YABBY5 (YAB5), as a central integrator of pollinator-attracting traits. YAB5 interacts with CRABS CLAW (CRC) during nectary initiation to specify nectary identity by repressing alternative floral organ fates. As flowers mature, YAB5 directly activates 4-α-glucanotransferase 2 (DPE2) to promote starch remobilization required for nectar secretion and promotes petal growth and flower opening. In petals, YAB5 directly engages an MYB111-dependent flavonoid pathway that generates UV nectar guides, while indirectly influencing floral volatile emission. Disrupting YAB5, DPE2, or MYB111 reduces pollinator visitation. Together, these findings reveal how a developmental regulator couples organ specification with organ-specific metabolic programs to synchronize floral rewards and signals at anthesis.

abstract: Cells resist viral infection by triggering rapid and sensitive innate immune responses, initiated by cytoplasmic viral sensor proteins (CyVSP), retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA-5), and protein kinase R (PKR). Our single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary viral genome input, significantly more than one, which we define as the virion input threshold for replication (VITREP). This threshold varies depending on viruses and cell types, independently of viral protein synthesis. Through mathematical modeling and experimental testing, we uncover that supra-unitary viral genome quantities activate negative feedback regulators (NFR) of CyVSP, including death-associated protein kinase 1 (DAPK1), Rio kinase 3 (RIOK3), and protein phosphatase 2 regulatory subunit alpha (PPP2R2A), that suppress innate immune responses and allow replication. We validate key predictions of our model, namely that downregulating NFR reduces replication, whereas upregulating NFR or coinfecting cells promotes replication. Together, these findings reveal a fundamental mechanism governing viral infectivity and tissue tropism.

abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion and multiple deletions frequently coexist in mitochondrial disease, neurodegeneration, and aging, yet how the two relate and why deletions accumulate focally remain unresolved. Here, longitudinal bulk and in situ analyses of Mpv17 -/- murine muscle reveal that a compensatory rise in mitochondrial transcripts per mtDNA initially offsets severe, uniform mtDNA depletion, preserving the respiratory chain. However, this response carries a delayed cost: by six months transcripts decline, mtDNA deletions emerge, and respiratory-deficient fibers appear. Paradoxically, fibers harboring deletions accumulate supra-physiological amounts of mtDNA, despite prior depletion. This expansion is invariably accompanied by elevated Hsp60, and the same holds in human mitochondrial myopathy. We propose that depletion reprograms mitochondrial DNA and RNA metabolism, inadvertently promoting deletion formation and creating an Hsp60-high fiber state permissive for clonal expansion. Therefore, depletion and multiple deletions can be sequential phases of a common degenerative process, relevant also to aging and neurodegeneration.

abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

abstract: Alveolar macrophages (AMs) undergo functional reprogramming that critically regulates lung inflammation. Although mitophagy is essential for mitochondrial quality control, its role in macrophage functional reprogramming during acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains unclear. Here, we identify the nuclear receptor Nr1h4 (FXR) as a transcriptional regulator of mitophagy in AMs. FXR activation transcriptionally upregulates serine palmitoyltransferase long chain base subunit 2 (Sptlc2), thereby enhancing mitophagy and promoting an anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype under inflammatory conditions. The FXR/Sptlc2 axis reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediator production while increasing anti-inflammatory markers. Conversely, FXR deficiency impairs mitophagy, exacerbates pulmonary inflammation, and aggravates lung injury in vivo. These findings establish the FXR/Sptlc2 axis as a regulator of mitochondrial quality control and macrophage functional reprogramming and identify it as a potential therapeutic target in ARDS.

abstract: Avian influenza viruses of the H5Nx subtype pose persistent pandemic threats. Here, we immunized rhesus macaques with an H5N6 vaccine and obtained 30 H5-reactive monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). Three IgG mAbs, 3CF5, 3BG3, and 3BE7, demonstrated potent neutralizing activity against multiple H5Nx viruses and conferred protection in a lethal mouse challenge model. Notably, 3CF5 exhibited broad neutralization against H5Nx viruses spanning 1997-2024, including contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 strains associated with an ongoing outbreak in dairy cattle. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis revealed that 3CF5 targets a conserved non-receptor-binding epitope on the hemagglutinin (HA) head, spanning the vestigial esterase domain and an adjacent lateral surface. 3CF5 mediates neutralization primarily through inhibiting membrane fusion and also possesses antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Furthermore, isotype conversion of 3CF5-IgG to mucosal secretory IgA1 (sIgA1) enhanced neutralization potency against H5N1 viruses up to 128-fold, highlighting the advantage of sIgA1 as a nasally administered prophylactic agent.

abstract: Proteins shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm through the nuclear pore and via nuclear transport receptors, termed importins and exportins. Although genetic alterations involving nucleoporins are enriched in pediatric, adolescent, and young adult (AYA) acute myeloid leukemia (AML), nucleocytoplasmic transport has not been extensively studied in this disease. We discover that genes encoding nucleocytoplasmic transport pathway components (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes [KEGG]: hsa03013) are enriched in AML cells from younger patients (≤40 years). Within this pathway, CSE1L is the highest expressed exportin in pediatric/AYA AML and shows minimal expression in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). CSE1L depletion reduces leukemic cell growth, proliferation, and clonogenic capacity, targeting leukemia stem cells while sparing normal HSCs. Mechanistically, we identify a novel Ran-GTP-dependent role for CSE1L in regulating pre-60S ribosomal subunit export in AML. Collectively, these data identify nucleocytoplasmic transport and ribosomal subunit export as enriched dependencies in pediatric/AYA AML and establish CSE1L-mediated export as a leukemic vulnerability.

abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) brainstem cell group is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates and influences both mind (cognition) and body (cardiorespiratory, metabolic, and immune functions) via two-putatively distinct-spontaneous activity patterns. Yet, the degree to which spontaneous LC firing rates and patterns are homogeneous across species has never been assessed due to inherently limited sample sizes. To remedy this, we pooled cross-species data from 20 laboratories to show that firing rates differ across species and are modulated by sex, age, and type of in vitro or in vivo preparation. Contrary to the prevailing dual-mode firing pattern schema, we observed patterns spread across a low-dimensional manifold, with subregions enriched for specific biological factors and neurodegenerative disease models. Our findings show considerable diversity in an ancestral vertebrate neuromodulatory system.

abstract: The plant slow anion channel SLAH3 regulates essential physiological processes, including stomatal closure and stress responses, yet the structural mechanism underlying its activation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the activation mechanism of SLAH3 by determining cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the wild-type (WT) channel and gain-of-function mutants identified through a targeted mutagenesis screen of pore-lining residues. Notably, the L400A mutant was captured in a dilated, open-like conformation, in contrast to the auto-inhibited WT channel. Structural comparisons revealed concerted rearrangements of the pore-lining transmembrane helices and intracellular regulatory elements. The observations point to an activation model in which displacement of the intracellular auto-inhibitory module relieves pore occlusion, triggering conformational changes that propagate from the intracellular loop to pore-lining segments, ultimately widening the entrance for anion transport. Therefore, our study provides a structural framework for understanding SLAH3 regulation and advances our understanding of nitrate signaling and stress adaptation in plants.

abstract: Inferring hidden cellular dynamics from static single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data remains a critical challenge. We review 16 computational methods that define cell potency under different, sometimes contrasting, assumptions. On the basis of how they summarize gene expression into a potency measure, we categorize them into average-based, entropy-based, and knowledge-based methods. Using a unified set of mathematical notations, we detail their methodologies, explain key similarities and differences within and between categories, and summarize usage complexities. Given the diversity of methods, community benchmark datasets at single-cell resolution and careful sensitivity analyses are crucial for evaluating methods from multiple angles and potentially improving stability and generalizability. This article provides a basis for method benchmarking and highlights the remaining challenge of comparing methods for inferring pseudotime trajectories, RNA velocities, and cell potency.

abstract: Upon infecting a bacterial cell, a lytic bacteriophage commandeers the host's resources to replicate, before lysing the cell to release new virions. As phages are obligate parasites, each stage of the infection process depends on the physiological parameters of the host cell. Given the inherent physiological variability within a population of genetically identical bacterial cells, we ask how the phage infection dynamic reflects such heterogeneity. Here, we introduce a time-lapse imaging assay for investigating the dynamics of individual infection steps by a single T7 phage on a single bacterium. This high-throughput, time-resolved assay enables us to monitor the infection progression simultaneously in multiple cells, uncovering substantial heterogeneity at each step and revealing correlations between infection dynamics and the physiological state of the infected cell. Simulations of competing phage populations reveal that heterogeneity in infection dynamics can significantly impact phage fitness, highlighting it as a potential evolutionary driver of phage-bacteria interactions. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

abstract: The US House's approval of the Sunshine Protection Act has revived the debate between permanent daylight saving time (DST) and standard time (ST). Permanent DST would push school start times before sunrise in many regions. Health, sleep, and scientific organizations favor permanent ST because it keeps solar, biological, and social time better aligned, 1 which matters most for children and adolescents, whose rigid school schedules already conflict with their biological night and are linked to poor sleep and reduced cognitive and academic performance. 2 , 3 , 4 The safety consequences of the proposed change remain unquantified, but for children, morning light availability matters most, since most return home in daylight regardless of clock policy. Using real school start times for 14 states that have approved permanent DST 5 and local sunrise times, we counted pre-sunrise commutes to school under each clock regime. Across the 14 states analyzed, permanent DST would require pre-sunrise departures for most of the winter, adding approximately 356 million days of pre-sunrise travel events among school-aged children (child days) relative to the current system (seasonally alternating between ST and DST). Applying the same approach nationwide, permanent DST would add more than 2 billion dark-morning commutes yearly. Analyzing a decade of national fatal crash records, we found higher odds of pedestrian involvement in dark-morning crashes than light-morning ones (odds ratio [OR] 1.77) and among pedestrians aged 5-18 (OR 2.22). Permanent DST would expose many more children to elevated pedestrian-crash risk, evidence that is relevant to the US' choice of a time standard.

abstract: The evolutionary success of spiders is often attributed to their stunning ability to produce and utilize silk, but the potential link between the molecular and phenotypic basis of silk production and spider diversification is seldom tested in a robust dated phylogenetic framework. Here, we provide a macroevolutionary context for testing hypotheses by reconstructing and dating the spider tree of life using genomic and transcriptomic data. We searched exhaustively for members of the spider silk protein (spidroin) gene family from omics data and identified them in an iterative phylogenetic pipeline. Four distinct new types of spidroins with atypical sequence characteristics are discovered to be widespread in true spiders with the potential to affect silk properties, as inferred by our phylogenetic generalized linear mixed model and phylogenetic generalized least squares analyses. Combining our robust dated phylogenomic tree of spiders and a comprehensive spidroin dataset, a comprehensive picture of spidroin evolution is revealed. By performing state speciation and extinction analyses, we discovered that only the presence of aggregate gland is linked to a higher diversification rate among all binary spidroin-related characters, while the speciation rate of spiders is dependent on the number of ampullate-gland-associated-atypical spidroin types, silk gland types, total spidroin copies, and total spidroin types.
