abstract: We sought to better understand the neural representation of visual motion acceleration. A straightforward estimation of acceleration would involve calculating the rate of change of velocity, which itself would be calculated from change in position over time. As it is well-established that neurons in area MT encode velocity, the brain could thus indirectly estimate acceleration by calculating the change in MT's velocity representations. An alternative mechanism, however, could operate more rapidly and directly. In this case, the brain could exploit interactions between MT's standard motion encoding and idiosyncratic temporal dynamics of neural responses. Such direct decoding would thus exploit nonlinearities usually ignored in studies of MT coding. We tested between these two theories by measuring from ensembles of MT neurons while two male awake fixating macaques viewed linearly accelerating motion stimuli. Direct decoding of acceleration from MT was possible on faster time scales, and could be done with higher fidelity, than indirect decoding. Distinct motion acceleration information could thus be efficiently read out from rich and heterogeneous MT ensemble responses, regardless of the mechanisms that give rise to various forms of motion tuning that it exhibits. A similar analysis of activity in the medial superior temporal area (MST) did not suggest that this later stage of motion processing has a more refined acceleration representation. Together, these results suggest that the brain may opportunistically exploit nonlinear idiosyncrasies of neural responses to efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information on fast time scales, instead of performing explicit calculation of certain variables. Significance Statement This study aims to understand if linear acceleration information of visual motion is extracted and represented in primate visual motion areas MT and MST. By combining large-scale multi-area neuronal recordings, population-level analyses, and a rich set of moving stimuli, we show that linear acceleration can be decoded from MT activity. Specifically, our results demonstrate that (1) motion acceleration is encoded in MT, and can be directly and quickly decoded from MT ensemble activity, and (2) area MST, despite being a later stage of motion processing, does not refine acceleration representations. These findings call for revisiting how brain areas might efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information from the environment and highlight the importance of temporal dynamics in visual motion processing.

abstract: The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior. Significance Statement The habenula - an epithalamic brain region - plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

abstract: Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition. Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

abstract: The process of forming a decision gives rise to an estimate of its quality or likelihood of success. This graded sense of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, but a neural mechanism linking subjective confidence to formation of the next decision has not been identified. We trained two male rhesus macaques to report a perceptual choice and simultaneous confidence judgment in a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task. Monkeys were more likely to repeat a rewarded choice when they reported low confidence on the previous trial, and showed greater changes in RT after a surprising outcome (low-confidence correct or high-confidence error). Neural activity in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) encoded the previous trial's choice and confidence more strongly after a low-confidence correct trial, and the strength of history encoding was correlated with a trial-by-trial estimate of choice bias. Ramping dynamics of the decoded decision variable also depended systematically on the conjunction of confidence and reward on the previous trial, in a manner that reflected individual differences between animals. The findings suggest that LIP not only reflects the formation of the current decision but could participate in confidence-guided learning via adjustments of the subsequent decision process. Significance statement Decision confidence is of primary interest in the study of metacognition, yet it also plays a key role in learning, serving as a graded prediction of accuracy that modulates the response to feedback. Reanalyzing data from nonhuman primates performing a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task with explicit confidence reports, we found that adjustments of choice bias and RT were gated by the animal's self-reported confidence on the previous trial. The interaction of confidence and outcome (reward or punishment) was reflected in the activity of parietal (LIP) neurons on the subsequent trial, in ways largely consistent with the behavioral effects. The results and accompanying computational model suggest plausible functional links between the neuronal substrates of perceptual decision making and reinforcement learning.

abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration. Significance Statement How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.

abstract: When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream. Significance Statement Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8-13 Hz) and beta (14-30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels. Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.

abstract: After spinal cord injury, clinical management aims to support tissue perfusion, but current methods rely on the indirect control of arterial blood pressure without direct measurement of the local blood flow. This limits the ability to tailor drug delivery to the injured tissue. Here, we show that spinal cord blood flow can be regulated using a closed-loop controller that adjusts vasopressor infusion on the basis of real-time ultrasound flow measurement. We characterize the dynamic relationship between drug infusion, arterial pressure and spinal cord blood flow, and we use these data to design a feedback controller that targets a predefined flow level. We validate the system in simulations, implement the controller in real time in rodents and translate it to pigs. We show that the controller reduced blood flow deviations and variability compared with constant dosing and supported functional recovery in a rodent survival model. These results show a closed-loop spinal cord perfusion control strategy that leverages clinically available measurements and pharmacological interventions, supporting its translation to clinical settings for the management of acute spinal cord injury.

abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) have an elevated risk of autoimmune disease, particularly celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and autoimmune hypothyroidism. In DS, thymi show characteristic structural and cellular changes, but the connection between these and the propensity to autoimmune disease is still unclear. Here we present a cell atlas from single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics of age-matched thymi from infants with and without DS, which might contribute to filling this knowledge gap. DS does not significantly alter CD34 + diversity in the thymus; however, the gene expression changes we observe indicate altered differentiative potential in DS CD34 + cells. Although many genes involved in T-cell development and function (including USP16 , RUNX1 and ETS2 ) are located on chromosome 21, several important T cell regulatory genes that are located on other chromosomes also change in DS. In contrast, CD34 - DS thymocytes are characterised by maturation defects. CD34 + progenitors and proliferating DP thymocytes are in a functional state of chronic interferon activation. In summary, we identify several notable differences in key functional cellular subsets and pathways within the DS thymus, providing insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of the thymic environment for this genetic condition.

abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

abstract: When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

abstract: The gut microbiota dysbiosis is a key factor leading to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Darutigenol (DL) is a natural compound with limited oral bioavailability but potent anti-inflammatory activity. However, its ameliorative efficacy in colitis and precise mechanism remain unexplored. This study demonstrated through multi-omics analysis and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) experiments that the alleviation of colitis in male mice by DL is dependent on the gut microbiota. Mechanistically, DL specifically enriches the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila ( A. muciniphila ), which alleviates colitis by promoting the synthesis of proline. Interestingly, DL was found to promote the growth of A. muciniphila in the gut by targeting indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Additionally, exogenous proline supplementation alleviated murine colitis by downregulating the IL-17 signaling pathway and its downstream cascades. Our findings reveal that DL ameliorates colitis by inhibiting IDO1 expression to drive A. muciniphila expansion and proline synthesis, and highlights the potential of DL for the treatment of IBD.

abstract: Acute and chronic exposure to elevated temperatures associated with Global Climate Change (GCC) threatens the structure and function of host-associated microbiomes, yet predicting microbial responses to heat stress remains challenging. We exposed two lines of the sea anemone, Exaiptasia diaphana , to acute and chronic thermal stress to quantify the impacts on cnidarian physiology and microbiome composition. Acute exposure caused rapid algal bleaching that was paired with pronounced shifts in bacteriome structure in both lines within 14 days of thermal exposure. Chronic exposure significantly affected the population structure, photo-physiology and bacteriome composition in only one host line, suggesting acclimation capacity depends on host-algal genetic backgrounds. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of 493 individuals sampled across 180 days, we found that sampling date explained nine-fold more variation in the microbiome composition than temperature exposure. Despite this temporal variation, we identified 16 indicator taxa that consistently changed in relative abundance under thermal stress. These taxa became central hubs in microbial association networks with increasing levels of thermal stress, suggesting they played key roles in bacteriome reorganization. As many of these taxa were present in other cnidarians, including reef-building corals, they may represent targets for conservation strategies that aim to enhance resilience on reefs.

abstract: The plasmid-mediated tigecycline resistance gene tet (X4) threatens the efficacy of tigecycline. While prevalent in Escherichia coli across diverse ecological niches, its evolutionary trajectory in Salmonella remains underappreciated. Here, we conducted nationwide genomic surveillance of 42403 clinical nontyphoidal Salmonella isolates collected from diarrheal patients in China between 2014 and 2025, of which 102 were tet (X4)-positive. Although the overall prevalence remained low, detection showed a statistically significant upward trend over 2019-2025. Importantly, the newly accrued 2025 data were broadly consistent with short-term forecasts generated by the beta regression model, providing partial support for short-term trend consistency. Genomic analyses showed that tet (X4) remained concentrated in ST34 but was also detected in additional sequence types, including ST469, ST8971, ST11 and one isolate with an unassigned ST, across multiple provinces, indicating broader geographic representation and genetic diversification. Plasmid analyses likewise revealed broader replicon diversity, with the dominant IncHI1A/IncHI1B/IncFIA background accompanied by less frequent IncHI2/IncHI2A, IncI1(Alpha) and IncFIA/IncFIB/IncFIC. Phylogenetic analyses further revealed shared clustering of the dominant plasmid background across host species and bacterial genera, consistent with cross-host and cross-genus circulation.

abstract: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is a mucosal yeast infection, mostly caused by Candida albicans , where symptoms are driven by inflammation. The onset of VVC is instigated by C. albicans pathogenicity, but the underlying causes of disease-driving hyperinflammation remain incompletely resolved. We found that vaginal albumin concentrations are higher in women with recurrent VVC and during experimental VVC in mice. These albumin levels correlated with inflammatory cytokines in vaginal lavages. While the abundance of this serum protein in the vagina can be a hallmark of inflammation-induced vascular permeability, we reveal molecular mechanisms by which albumin can also drive inflammation. Albumin increased NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human macrophages elicited by C. albicans . This was associated with increased resistance of C. albicans to macrophage-mediated clearance in the presence of albumin. Further, albumin increased the expression of fungal secreted aspartic protease 1, which we identified as the effector driving inflammasome activation and IL-1β responses in vitro and in an in vivo VVC model. Moreover, neutrophils also exhibited impaired clearance of C. albicans in the presence of albumin. Collectively, vaginal albumin may not only be a consequence of inflammation of the vaginal mucosa, but also can drive C. albicans- induced hyperinflammatory IL-1β responses that underlie immunopathology in VVC.

abstract: Emergence of antimicrobial resistance is a pressing global issue. Although myriads of mechanisms for survival against antimicrobial pressure have surfaced, one key strategy is the structural modification of peptidoglycan, the main defense line in Gram-positive bacteria e.g., notorious pathogen Staphylococcus aureus . Here we show that the recently identified peptidoglycan hydrolase (PGH) LytU is an unusual catalyst in the lysostaphin (M23B) family of zinc-endopeptidases that hydrolyze the glycyl-glycine peptide bond in S. aureus . Unlike any other PGH recognized thus far, LytU hydrolyzes the isopeptide bond between the lysine ε amino group and pentaglycine, thus functioning as a bridge-link hydrolase. We discovered that LytM and LytU are functionally non-redundant, and they contribute to the cell wall remodeling at different stages of PG maturation. Additionally, we demonstrate that LytU particularly targets the PG precursor, pGly-Lipid II, and its overexpression leads to growth inhibition and a less densely cross-linked cell wall, which increases susceptibility to lysostaphin. Interestingly, LytU expression enhances resistance to the glycopeptide vancomycin, the drug of last resort against S. aureus .

abstract: Listeria monocytogenes navigates a crowded intracellular environment by recruiting host factors to its surface in order to hijack the host actin cytoskeleton for motility and cell-to-cell spread. Although these types of Listeria -host interactions are critical for infection, systematic characterization of this interface has been limited. Here, we implement the biotin ligase split-TurboID to profile host proteins recruited to the surface of L. monocytogenes during intracellular infection. We show that the host deubiquitinase CYLD is enriched at the pathogen surface. While CYLD promotes infection by suppressing innate immunity in macrophages, how L. monocytogenes recruits and appropriates CYLD function in other cell types has remained unclear. We demonstrate that L. monocytogenes uses the secreted effector Internalin C (InlC) to redirect CYLD to M1-linked linear ubiquitin at the bacterial poles. Despite its localization, CYLD does not deubiquitinate bacteria or regulate autophagic clearance in epithelial cells. Instead, CYLD and InlC protect L. monocytogenes from IFN-γ- and RNF213-dependent restriction of cell-to-cell spread. Overall, our work profiling the bacterial surface-host interactome has identified a mechanism by which InlC spatially reprograms CYLD activity to promote cell-to-cell spread in epithelial cells. These findings highlight how L. monocytogenes exploits a host deubiquitinase to perform cell-type-specific functions during infection.

abstract: Conserved polyadenylation b3y poly(A) polymerases (PAPs) is essential for mRNA stability, yet its metabolic functions remain unclear. Here we identify a rare variant p.D469N (Asp469Asn) in Star-PAP present in lean individuals but absent in obese cases. Adipose-specific Star-PAP knockout mice develop progressive adipose tissue loss, hepatic steatosis, and severe insulin resistance, phenocopying human lipodystrophy. Mechanistically, Star-PAP directly binds the insulin receptor ( InsR ) mRNA 3’–UTR to stabilize its transcript. Both deletion of Star-PAP and p.D469N variant decrease InsR mRNA maturation. Star-PAP deficiency impairs insulin receptor signaling and adipocyte lipid storage, while restoring InsR in adipocytes partially ameliorates the lipodystrophic phenotypes. Notably, Star-PAP deficiency disrupts acetyl-CoA homeostasis secondary to insulin signaling defects, accompanied by reduced histone acetylation at fatty acid synthesis genes. Pyruvate supplementation effectively restores acetyl-CoA levels and histone acetylation, thereby rescuing the gene expression and lipogenesis. Together, our results identify Star-PAP-mediated RNA polyadenylation as a mechanism governing adipose mass, positioning Star-PAP as a key regulator of insulin receptor signaling and lipodystrophy.

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) offer potential advantages for clinical diagnosis over standard large language models (LLMs), yet their utility and safety remain unclear. Here we show, on AIMS-LDR, a long-context diagnostic reasoning benchmark built upon real-world electronic health records, covering six matched model pairs and 12 specialties, that LRMs generate over 34% more false positive diagnoses and show approximately 40% lower reproducibility than their LLM counterparts, while making more accurate primary diagnoses and more clinically relevant differentials. Experiments confirm this trade-off across prompt designs, model hyperparameters, and evaluation paradigms. A structured collaboration model, in which the LRM broadens diagnostic coverage and the clinician verifies reliability, increases diagnostic accuracy by 20% and reduces false positives by 44% in a 15-physician validation study. These results, obtained under controlled retrospective conditions, suggest that pairing LRM reasoning with physician oversight may support safer and more accurate diagnostic decision-making, warranting prospective validation before clinical deployment.

abstract: The rapid evolution of spermatogenesis limits the utility of mouse models for studying human spermatogenesis because some genes are absent or divergent in mice. Primate models face practical and ethical constraints, whereas tree shrews are closely related to primates and suitable for laboratory research. Here we integrate histology and single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from human, rhesus macaque, mouse and tree shrew testes to assess the tree shrew as a model of human spermatogenesis. We show that transcriptional landscapes in tree shrew spermatogenic cells, particularly late-stage spermatids, more closely resemble those of primates than mice. Conservation and enrichment analyses identify two core gene modules shared among humans, macaques and tree shrews but distinct in mice. Gene expression trajectories also align between tree shrews and primates, including for genes without murine orthologs. Immunostaining and RNA-FISH support representative expression patterns. These findings define contexts in which tree shrews can complement existing models of human spermatogenesis and male infertility.

abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses often use 3′ tRNA-like structures (TLSs) instead of poly(A) tails to capture the host translation machinery. While TLSs resemble canonical tRNAs and engage host factors, their ability to directly recruit ribosomes has remained unresolved. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy snapshots of the histidine-accepting TLS (TLS His ) from tobacco mosaic virus bound to the tobacco 60 S subunit, the 80 S ribosome, and the 80 S -tRNA i Met initiation complex. Across these states, TLS His is consistently anchored to the L1 stalk of 60 S , even under cycloheximide treatment, yet remains dynamic on the 40 S subunit. Structural analysis shows that TLS His transitions from the E-site to an adjacent Z-site to accommodate initiator tRNA. Functional assays show that TLS His preferentially associates with ribosomal subunits over polysomes and can substitute for a poly(A) tail to promote robust cap-dependent translation. These results provide structural and mechanistic evidence that the viral tRNA mimic exploits the tRNA-exit channel to stabilize initiation-competent ribosomes and drive poly(A)-independent translation.

abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling–Cell Painting (JUMP–CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

abstract: Analysis of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation can enable noninvasive disease detection by leveraging tissue-specific epigenetic differences between malignant and nonmalignant cells. However, such analyses can be confounded by the repair of jagged DNA fragment ends during double-stranded sequencing library preparation, which introduces spurious methylation signals into cfDNA molecules. Here we present JEEPERS, a framework to detect and correct jagged-end-induced methylation errors while preserving duplex integrity and native methylation patterns. We showed high fidelity for measuring tumor burden and demonstrated allele-specific methylation differences at recurrent somatic mutations, revealing a link between adjacent CpG methylation and EGFR / TP53 driver and resistance mutations. We further demonstrated enhanced diagnostic performance across liquid biopsy applications, including tumor-type-specific methylation profiles, hemimethylation profiling, epigenetic-clock-based age estimation and cell type deconvolution. By faithfully correcting end-repair errors, JEEPERS provides a versatile framework for integrating mutations and methylation features in cfDNA at high resolution, enabling more precise molecular profiling and disease monitoring.

abstract: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with various traits that influence individuals' experiences at work. While some may be experienced as challenging (e.g., when differences in executive function impact time management), others can be more positive (e.g., when curiosity motivates exploration and discovery). Plausibly, academia is a work environment where these positive aspects should be valued. However, ADHD is still often viewed from a medicalised perspective in workplace settings, despite the neurodiversity paradigm offering an alternative, non-pathologising way to frame these individual differences. Research has begun to explore employment experiences and outcomes for adults with ADHD; however, there is currently little data relevant to academic workplaces specifically. This qualitative study offers a critical realist analysis of interviews with early-career academics, seeking to understand first-person ADHD perspectives on establishing an academic career. Consistent with the neurodiversity paradigm, the analysis foregrounds (mis-)matches between individual 'neurotypes' and workplace environments. It also highlights an ecological view by exploring how ADHD matters both for individual careers and for collective knowledge production. Findings suggest that academia can, in principle, be a rewarding environment for ADHDers, though social and institutional pressures often inhibit this potential. Furthermore, having an 'ADHD neurotype' influences both individual career trajectories and wellbeing at work; at the same time, knowledge production at the collective level may benefit from the inclusion of ADHD academics. The findings are discussed in reference to ecological models of neurodiversity and their implications for universities aiming to facilitate neurodivergent contributions and inclusion at work.

abstract: The aim of video anomaly detection is to identify events that deviate significantly from normal behavior. The majority of the current methods for identifying anomalous behaviors rely primarily on frame reconstruction and frame prediction. However, due to the powerful representation and generation of deep neural networks, it is not sufficient to assume that anomaly events in the reconstruction methods have larger reconstruction errors. Likewise, prediction methods are not robust to noise, which can impact the effectiveness of anomaly detection. In this paper, we propose an anomaly detection method based on cascaded attention U-Nets, combining the advantages and balancing the disadvantages of the reconstruction methods and the prediction methods. Specifically, by integrating the spatial attention module and transformer-based channel attention module into the cascaded U-Nets, the weights of the spatial regions and the channel regions that represent background features can be decreased. Furthermore, to fully utilize the temporal information, a temporal shift module is incorporated into the prediction network to improve future frame prediction. Extensive experiments were conducted on several public benchmark datasets, such as the UCSD Ped dataset, the CUHK Avenue dataset, the ShanghaiTech dataset and the UCF-crime dataset. The results indicate that the proposed method can effectively enlarge the gaps between the normal events and the anomaly events, and achieve AUC 95.6% on the UCSD Ped2 dataset, 84.1% on the UCSD Ped1 dataset, 87.6% on the CUHK Avenue dataset, 75.1% on the ShanghaiTech dataset, 73.5% on the UCF-crime dataset, which outperform other previous state-of-the-art methods.

abstract: The dCas9 system has rapidly been developed into many tools to explore different aspects of the human genome; the high binding specificity, coupled with the inactive nuclease enzyme, allows for precise recruitment of molecules to specific sequences of DNA. We sought to exploit these capabilities to create a tool for assessing the real-time proximity of two DNA sequences within a biological system. By incorporating aptamers into gRNAs, dCas9 molecules can be used to recruit the β9 or β10 strands of split-NanoLuc® to specific DNA sequences and quantify the proximity of those sequences based on their ability to complex with the luciferase fragment (Δ11S) and produce luminescence. While many tools exist to detect a single DNA sequence, this system is uniquely capable of assessing how two DNA sequences interact with each other. As expected, we found that the interaction of two dCas9 molecules was affected by their linear distance from each other on dsDNA. Surprisingly, we found that their interaction was also strongly influenced by rotational orientation, even for sequences that are close together in linear space. This finding indicates that dCas9 rotational alignment is an important consideration for designing dCas9 systems that target multiple DNA sequences simultaneously. Beyond the findings presented herein, we believe this DNA proximity detection tool has the potential to be adapted for applications involving the proximity and orientation of two DNA sequences.

abstract: Brain tumors, which are abnormal growths in the brain or central spinal canal, represent a serious global health threat. In 2023, they were responsible for 94,390 cases and 18,990 deaths in the US. Early detection with Magnetic Resonance Imaging is critical for effective treatment and higher survival rates. In this paper, we propose a method for the classification and localization of brain tumors in magnetic resonance imaging. Our method is based on the application of convolutional neural networks and for this task, we introduce and design a new network called the CBP_Net. The experimental analysis includes the Standard_CNN, a network designed by the authors, and other state-of-the-art networks, i.e., MobileNet, DenseNet, InceptionV3, ResNet50 and EfficientNetB0. This study emphasizes both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The results demonstrate that the networks achieve optimal quantitative metrics: from 0.993 to 1.0 in accuracy. Qualitatively, we focus on visual explanations using Class Activation Mapping algorithms, specifically Grad-CAM and Score-CAM, to generate heatmaps highlighting relevant regions in the images. The Structural Similarity Index Measure is then employed to quantitatively measure the similarity between the heatmaps generated by the two CAM algorithms. This approach improves the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-driven brain tumor detection, helping clinicians diagnose.

abstract: The soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) graphically describes the significant hydraulic characteristics of unsaturated soil seepage. Several factors influence the SWCC of unsaturated soil, including temperature, void ratio, pore characteristics, particle composition, and load, with soil pore structure exerting a pivotal influence on SWCC. This study aimed to analyze the influence of pore structure on the SWCC of loess. The results showed that the shape of SWCC of loess is similar with varying pore structures under a fixed void ratio, with discrepancies in the air entry value(AEV) and decline sections. The void ratio of macro pores of intact loess exceeded that of remolded loess, in turn resulting in a larger AEV. There were fewer small pores and middle pores in the intact loess sample, whereas the remolded loess showed a greater decline rate after transitioning into an the unsaturated state. On the other hand, an increase in the size of the pores was observed in the loess following the drying-wetting cycles, whereas the number of smaller and middle-sized pores decreased. Similarly, there was an increase in AEV of loess following the drying-wetting cycles, with the gradual deceleration in the rate of decline in the unsaturated stage. The pore state parameters and fractal dimension of pore size distribution(PSD) were introduced into the V-G model based on the experimental results, with deriving a modified V-G model. The intact loess was predicted by remolded loess, and the loess after the drying-wetting cycles were predicted by loess before the drying-wetting cycles. The results showed that the modified V-G model is more effective in predicting the SWCC of intact loess and loess after the drying-wetting cycles.

abstract: Cross-condition bearing fault diagnosis often has to adapt to a new operating condition with only a few labelled target samples. This setting creates two coupled problems. First, the sparse target support set cannot describe the target fault distribution sufficiently. Second, the same fault class may occupy different feature regions across source and target conditions, which weakens source-domain pretrained classifiers. Existing methods usually improve few-shot learning or reduce domain shift, but they rarely enrich the labelled target-class representation before class-wise source-target alignment. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a target-domain augmentation and class-wise alignment framework for few-shot cross-condition bearing fault diagnosis. The rime optimization algorithm (RIME) is first used to optimize the variational mode decomposition (VMD) parameters K and α, and fault-sensitive components are selected using envelope entropy and adjacent modal-frequency overlap. The reconstructed signal is converted into symmetric dot pattern (SDP) images to provide a noise-suppressed polar representation. The fast generative adversarial network (FastGAN) then generates auxiliary target-domain SDP samples from the limited labelled target support set, making each target fault class less sparse. On this basis, class-wise maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD) is embedded into a Swin Transformer classifier to align source and target features within each known fault category. Experiments on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) and Xi'an Jiaotong University-Shenyang Blower Works (XJTU-SY) datasets show that the proposed framework improves target-domain few-shot adaptation, achieving 93.33% and 97.58% accuracy under the G20 and G50 XJTU-SY target-augmentation settings, respectively.

abstract: Stress is a major contributor to physical and mental health disorders, underscoring the need for reliable and interpretable detection systems. We present an interpretable multimodal deep learning framework that integrates electrocardiogram (ECG), electrodermal activity (EDA), and respiration signals using modality-specific neural architectures complemented by feature-based classical models. To ensure robustness and generalizability, the framework was evaluated under both subject-independent and subject-dependent protocols. Results show that multimodal fusion consistently outperformed single modalities, achieving 94.8% accuracy, 93.9% F1-score, and 0.97 AUC under subject-independent validation, compared with 86-91% accuracy for individual signals. In subject-dependent experiments, performance reached 97.2% accuracy and 96.8% F1-score. Comparative analysis with recent state-of-the-art methods demonstrated the competitiveness of our approach, while ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each modality and fusion strategy. Statistical significance testing with (p < 0.05) further validated the reliability of these gains. Importantly, interpretability analyses using Grad-CAM and attention visualization provided physiological insights, revealing that the model emphasizes clinically meaningful regions such as ECG R-peaks and phasic EDA fluctuations. By uniting high performance, robustness, and interpretability, this work advances stress detection research and offers a physiologically grounded framework for continuous mental health monitoring.

abstract: Photophobia encompasses a continuum of light-induced experiences from mild discomfort to overt pain and intolerance, yet clinical tools rarely quantify these distinctions, leaving many patients undiagnosed and untreated. This study employed the Ocular Photosensitivity Analyzer (OPA), a compact instrument for quantitative sensory testing (QST) with light, to investigate three perceptual levels in healthy adults: visual photosensitivity discomfort threshold (VPDT), visual photosensitivity pain threshold (VPPT), and an exploratory outcome, visual photosensitivity tolerance level (VPTol). Twenty-nine participants ages 19-34 underwent standardized OPA testing, during which they identified when light first became uncomfortable, painful, and intolerable. After each trial, participants rated the peak pain intensity (PI) and peak unpleasantness (UP) using visual analog scales. Measured illuminance values differed significantly across the perceptual levels (RM-ANOVA, N = 28, F(1.69, 45.6)=37.06, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.58; Mauchly's W = 0.82, p = 0.072), indicating sensory levels are differentiable. Post hoc t-tests revealed VPTol exceeded VPPT (N = 28, t(27)=-2.29, p = 0.030, dz = 0.43)), and both exceeded VPDT (VPTol: N = 29, t(28)=-7.69, p < 0.001, dz = 1.43, VPPT: N = 29, t(27)=-7.69, p < 0.001, dz = 1.47). Friedman's test revealed UP (N = 28, χ2(2)=17.64, p < 0.001, Kendall's W = 0.32) and PI (N = 28, χ2(2)=22.36, p < 0.001, Kendall's W = 0.40) differences across perceptual levels and post hoc Wilcoxon tests showed UP and PI increased between VPDT and VPPT (UP: N = 29, Z = -4.34, p < 0.001, r = 0.57, PI: N = 29, Z = -4.58, p < 0.001, r = 0.60) and UP increased between VPDT and VPTol (N = 28, Z = -2.92, p = 0.007, r = 0.39), suggesting that both affective and sensory dimensions of pain vary across perceptual levels. Although preliminary, these findings are consistent with a multidimensional framework of photophobia. Additionally, the OPA's ability to differentially quantify VPDT, VPPT, and VPTol offers a novel approach to characterize light sensitivity that may aid future assessment of abnormal light sensitivity.

abstract: Accurate prediction of loan defaulters through collaborative analysis of financial data across multiple institutions is critical for maintaining financial stability and strengthening credit risk management. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables organizations to train models without exchanging raw data, its reliance on a centralized server introduces serious trust concerns, including vulnerability to gradient inversion and membership inference attacks. Blockchain-based Federated Learning (BCFL) addresses these challenges by cryptographically protecting and aggregating model updates through a smart contract, thereby providing a tamper-resistant learning process. In spite of these security enhancements, current BCFL frameworks do not ensure sustained client participation in real-world settings. Moreover, while traditional incentive mechanisms promote truthful participation and discourage free-riding and malicious behavior, they mainly reward model utility and neglect privacy contribution. To mitigate this limitation, we propose BCFL-DAI-PUB, a blockchain-federated learning framework integrating an innovative Dynamic Adaptive Incentive (DAI) mechanism to achieve a Privacy-Utility Balance (PUB). The proposed DAI dynamically applies three complementary incentive components, such as SCAFFOLD-based correction, adaptive differential privacy (DP-Boost), and monetary rewards, to jointly optimize learning utility and privacy protection. This work promotes honest participation, discourages dishonest behavior, and enables rapid recovery from malicious attacks, thereby improving global convergence and overall model effectiveness. The proposed BCFL-DAI-PUB achieves a final AUC of 0.91, improving upon the HE-based BCFL-PS-HER baseline (0.86) by 1.06×. By replacing homomorphic encryption with adaptive differential privacy and combining it with a dynamic incentive mechanism, the proposed framework improves both efficiency and resilience over the baseline, which relies on static reputation-based coordination. Compared with the baseline BCFL-PS-HER model, BCFL-DAI-PUB recovers from malicious disruption 1.82× faster and achieves approximately 1.22× higher MIA resistance, while the baseline incurs approximately 1.09× higher communication overhead and 1.14× higher storage overhead. These results show that BCFL-DAI-PUB improves predictive performance, strengthens privacy protection, reduces system cost, and provides more robust operation in blockchain-enabled federated credit-risk modelling.

abstract: Cable-driven soft exosuits for gait assistance are predominantly sagittal-plane devices, yet pathological gait involves coordinated deviations across all three anatomical planes. This study experimentally evaluated whether cable-routing geometry alone, within a single-actuator hip exosuit, can produce measurable multiplanar hip effects during walking. Ten healthy, exosuit-experienced male adults walked on a treadmill under five conditions: one matched unpowered control and four powered configurations that paired single-plane and multi-plane cable routing with hip-flexion and hip-extension assistance. Three-dimensional hip kinematics were compared across conditions, and exosuit-generated hip torques were estimated from subject-specific musculoskeletal models. Multi-plane routing produced phase-dependent kinematic changes concentrated in the transverse plane. Relative to unassisted walking, multi-plane flexion assistance increased hip internal rotation (3.6°, p = 0.0002), multi-plane extension assistance increased hip external rotation (1.8°, p = 0.0095), and single-plane flexion assistance produced a smaller but significant increase in external rotation (1.1°, p = 0.0463). Frontal-plane differences were not significant for any comparison with unassisted walking, so the hypothesized larger frontal-plane deviations under multi-plane routing were not supported. Multi-plane routing also produced greater sagittal-plane hip excursion than single-plane routing. Overall gait-trajectory similarity between single-plane and multi-plane routing was comparable in most comparisons and differed significantly only in the hip frontal plane during extension assistance. The estimated torques indicated that multi-plane routing introduced larger frontal- and transverse-plane components while the sagittal-plane component remained dominant. These findings show that cable-routing geometry alone can shape phase-localized hip kinematics, reaching significance in the transverse plane, without adding actuators. The effect magnitudes were small and near the measurement uncertainty of the capture system. The all-male, exosuit-experienced sample limits generalizability, so relevance to clinical populations remains to be tested. Cable-routing geometry is therefore proposed as a candidate rather than an established design variable for multi-dimensional assistance in soft exosuits.

abstract: CD47, a transmembrane protein with well-established immune and neurodevelopmental roles, was recently identified as an abundant presynaptic protein in humans, non-human primates, and mice. To investigate how Cd47 influences neuronal stress and injury, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of hippocampi from wild-type (WT) and Cd47 knockout (KO) mice exposed to kainic acid (KA) at convulsive (KA25; 25 mg/kg) or subconvulsive (KA3; 3 mg/kg) doses. Integrating cell-type annotations with Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed distinct neuronal and glial gene modules whose co-expression structure differed by genotype and by KA exposure. Notably, certain modules showed KA-associated changes in co-expression structure only in Cd47-deficient cells. Enrichment analyses of these modules highlighted translational, bioenergetic, and synaptic gene sets. Comparing transcriptome-wide distributions using Wasserstein distance demonstrated that vehicle-treated KO cells most closely resembled WT cells exposed to KA3, of all fifteen pairwise comparisons. These findings suggest that Cd47 loss shifts the hippocampal transcriptome toward a state resembling mild excitotoxic stress, implicating Cd47 as a candidate regulator of neuronal stress adaptation and providing a hypothesis for testing that role.

author_details.name: Christian Mesía-Montenegro

abstract: Ceramic differentiation can involve altered associations among continuing attributes without wholesale categorical replacement. At Wacheqsa, Chavín de Huántar, Peru, this study compares ware composition, decorative techniques, and their associations in 1,308 decorated or surface-treated sherd observations from five archaeological contexts. Early Platforms and Water Flood constitute the earlier Urabarroid aggregate; Stone Rooms, Midden, and Late Platforms constitute the later Janabarroid aggregate. These labels describe ceramic affinities within pre-existing context sets, whose stratigraphic networks are only partly connected and whose formation histories differ. On identical common support of nine wares and six techniques (n = 334/822), ware-margin Hellinger distance is 0.430 (95% fixed-count interval 0.392-0.481), technique-margin distance is 0.588 (0.551-0.634), and joint distance is 0.734 (0.714-0.793). A homogeneous-association model rejects a common ware-technique association after aggregate-specific margins are fitted (G2 = 118.59; pboot = 0.0001); the result persists without Midden (G2 = 90.16; pboot = 0.0001). Early Platforms differs from each later context, and stamping/impression is prominent in all three later samples, although those contexts retain distinct joint profiles. Nine of eleven ware categories occur in both aggregates, with pronounced differences in the association of polished wares with incision and stamping/impression. The contrast is consistent with differing decorated repertoires across activity and depositional settings, including contexts associated with collective consumption. Local superpositions and the published chronology support a temporal interpretation, but the contribution of elapsed time cannot be separated from differences in activity and deposition.

abstract: Ischemic heart disease remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Its diagnosis largely relies on detecting dynamic changes in the ST segment of the electrocardiogram (ECG). However, alterations in other ECG waves and intervals have also been reported. One factor that is often overlooked is the presence of a prior myocardial infarction and its influence on the myocardial response to a new ischemic event. This study aimed to quantify the magnitude and temporal dynamics of ECG changes during acute myocardial ischemia and to evaluate how a previous infarction modifies these changes. Twelve-lead ECG recordings obtained before and during acute ischemia induced by percutaneous coronary intervention in one of the three major coronary arteries were analyzed. Dynamic heartbeat averages were computed to extract and track features related to ECG depolarization (QRS width, amplitude, and area) and repolarization (T-wave amplitude and area, ST-segment deviation and area, and T-to-QRS amplitude ratio). The results show that, beyond ST-segment deviation, multiple ECG markers evolve over time during coronary artery occlusion. Repolarization features showed earlier and more pronounced alterations than depolarization features, reaching approximately 37-fold and 23-fold changes at 4 minutes of occlusion compared with baseline, respectively. Males showed faster and more sustained ST increases (up to ~47-fold vs ~30-fold in females); older patients had abrupt early ST peaks (~38-fold at ~2 min after occlusion), whereas younger patients exhibited a more gradual increase. Moreover, patients with a prior infarction showed a stronger association between ECG changes and both the extent and severity of ischemia, reaching maximum correlation coefficients of 0.75 for repolarization markers and 0.57 for depolarization markers. Distinct spatial lead patterns were also identified according to the occluded artery and the presence of a prior infarction. In conclusion, acute ischemia induces dynamic changes across multiple ECG markers beyond the ST segment, where repolarization changes precede and exceed depolarization. These responses are modulated by age and sex; furthermore, prior infarction tightens their correlation with ischemic burden and alters spatial lead patterns.

abstract: This randomized, statistician-blinded, parallel-group clinical trial will compare the effectiveness of three bone-augmentation techniques applied to the posterior mandible using the cortical shell approach. Eighty-seven participants will be randomly allocated into three groups (autogenous, xenogeneic, or allogeneic cortical shells), each combined with a 1:1 mixture of autogenous bone chips and biomaterial. Participants may contribute one or two eligible posterior mandibular sites; however, the unit of analysis for the primary outcome will be the participant, using a participant-level summary (mean value when two sites are treated). The study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06661447). Recruitment has not yet begun. The single primary endpoint is horizontal bone gain (mm) at 6 months, evaluated by cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Additional CBCT assessments at 3 and 12 months will be analyzed as secondary longitudinal outcomes. Volumetric and morphometric analyses will be performed through a standardized digital workflow integrating intraoral scanning, CBCT segmentation, and surface registration. Secondary outcomes will include bone density, surgical duration, and postoperative inflammation. Based on a previous CBCT-based randomized clinical trial with a related horizontal ridge-augmentation methodology, assuming a pooled standard deviation of approximately 1.12 mm and a clinically relevant between-group difference of 1.0 mm, 26 evaluable participants per group are required to achieve approximately 81.5% power for each prespecified primary comparison using a conservative two-sided α of 0.025 for sample-size planning. To allow for an anticipated 10% attrition rate, 29 participants will be recruited per group, resulting in a total planned sample of 87 participants. The primary analysis will use an ANCOVA model adjusted for baseline ridge width. This study aims to generate controlled, quantitative evidence on the volumetric and clinical performance of different cortical graft materials for posterior mandibular reconstruction. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06661447. The registry record will be updated before recruitment begins.

abstract: Access to supportive care remains a major public health concern. Digital tools are increasingly used in healthcare to address supportive care needs. It is essential to understand the needs and perspectives of the end users of these tools, including patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals (HCPs), to design and implement an option that effectively supports cancer patients and their relatives. This study was conducted to document and compare the perspectives of patients, relatives, and HCPs in France to identify perceived facilitators and barriers to the use of digital supportive care tools, as well as these individuals' expectations regarding tool development. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with three different groups: 38 patients with cancer (including two unusable interviews), 20 relatives, and 43 HCPs. The interviews were analysed using textual statistical analysis in IRaMuTeQ. Four classes emerged from the analysis: (1) cancer experience, (2) patient care, (3) imagination and positioning in the conceptualisation of the digital tool: the content, and (4) tool shape: the container. Across the three groups, there was broad agreement regarding identified needs and potential solutions. Participants did not conceptualise digital supportive tools as a care or treatment device, but rather as an informational and reflexive space, centred on the ability to seek, think, choose, and express oneself, while preserving human mediation. This finding is important because it highlights a shift in digital health toward a customisable empowerment tool that integrates patients and relatives, accounts for usage barriers, and is designed as an optional complement rather than a prescriptive solution. The results also highlight the importance of user-centred, accessible, and tailored approaches in tool development.

abstract: Proteins on the cell membrane cluster to respond to extracellular signals; for example, adhesion proteins cluster to enhance extracellular matrix sensing. The maturation of such receptor clusters may require additional adhesome proteins to adapt and reinforce extracellular signal sensing. However, it has been unclear whether the genes encoding these proteins share a spatial organization in the nucleus. Using the adhesome as an example, we show that subsets of genes that code for adhesome proteins exhibit relative spatial clustering and co-regulation in distinct locations within the nucleus. We use Hi-C maps and RNA-seq data from adherent cells to map the correspondence between adhesome gene localization and their expression. Interestingly, we find that the genes encoding several transcription factors, cofactors, and chromatin regulators that regulate these genes are also co-localized with the adhesome gene loci, thereby potentially suggesting a link between the extracellular matrix sensing machinery and gene expression. Additionally, we validate the spatial sub-clustering of adhesome gene loci using MERFISH data and DNA-FISH experiments. Collectively, our results support an association between adhesome gene organization and regulatory state, with a possible role in cellular signal sensing.

abstract: Background War profoundly affects quality of life (QOL) by disrupting daily routines, damaging infrastructure, and creating fear and uncertainty. This study aimed to develop and preliminarily validate the Arabic Quality of Life During War Scale (AQOL-War). Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted in Sudan during wartime from June 11 to September 10, 2024. Data were collected through an anonymous online survey and face-to-face interviews. Cronbach's alpha was used to measure the tool's internal consistency. We assessed face, content, concurrent, and structural validity, along with measurement invariance. Results Among 635 participants, the mean age was 27.9 ± 9.1 years, 72.1% were females, 65.4% lived in urban areas, 67.1% lived in their own house, 71.5% were single, 70.1% had a university education, 71.7% were not currently employed, 19.2% were from Khartoum State, and 21.3% reported losing a family member during the recent war. Exploratory factor analysis yielded a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) of 0.889, and Bartlett's test was significant (χ² = 4965.76, p < 0.001). Three factors (environment and security, psychological health, and physical health) with eigenvalues > 1 were extracted with a cumulative variance explained of 41.8%. Confirmatory factor analysis showed satisfactory model fit (χ2 = 831.36, p < 0.001) with good fit indices [root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.06, root mean square residual (RMR) = 0.04, comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.916, goodness of fit index (GFI) = 0.936, Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) = 0.905, and non-normed fit index (NNFI) = 0.905]. The overall Cronbach's alpha for the quality-of-life tool was 0.93; values for "environment and security", "psychological health", and "physical health" were 0.94, 0.84, and 0.83, respectively. Conclusions The AQOL-War demonstrated satisfactory preliminary validity, reliability, and configural and metric invariance. It may provide a contextually relevant measure for researchers and clinicians working with Arabic-speaking populations affected by war. Further cross-context replication and longitudinal evaluation are needed.

abstract: Background Post‑stroke fatigue (PSF) affects approximately 50% of stroke survivors and is one of the most common and disabling post‑stroke sequelae. Digital and technology‑enabled approaches have attracted increasing attention in the field of stroke rehabilitation, including mobile health applications (mHealth), wearable devices, virtual reality (VR), remote rehabilitation, artificial intelligence (AI), and neuromodulation technologies. However, no comprehensive scoping review has systematically mapped the full spectrum of evidence on digital and technology‑enabled approaches for PSF. Methods This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews, be guided by the Population, Concept, Context (PCC) framework, and be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta‑Analysis Protocols (PRISMA‑P) and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta‑Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA‑ScR). Eight electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and PsycINFO) and five gray literature sources (OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and Google Scholar) will be searched. Two reviewers will use NoteExpress to remove duplicates and manage references, and will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts. After pilot testing, data will be extracted independently by the two reviewers. Synthesis will involve descriptive numerical summaries and inductive qualitative content analysis. Inter‑rater agreement will be assessed during a calibration phase. The expected output is an evidence map organized by approach category and purpose (assessment, monitoring, prevention, and treatment), which will identify knowledge gaps and guide future research. Registration This protocol has been registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). Registration DOI (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/4WMEK).

abstract: This work constructs a fractional-order model to describe the dynamics of particle chains with asymmetric coupling subject to non-uniform viscoelastic media and an asymmetric periodic potential. The effects of multiple control parameters on the collective directed motion are systematically investigated. Numerical results reveal that the fractional-order coupled system can achieve directed transport in the absence of external forces and noise driving. Under suitable coupling strengths, the directed transport velocity of the particle chain generally rises as the fractional order increases. We also find that the average velocity of the particle chain exhibits generalized resonance responses with varying system parameters, featuring single-peak, double-peak and multi-peak resonant behaviors. Such resonant behaviors are sensitive to system parameters and originate from the competition between fractional power-law memory and interparticle coupling. Reverse directed transport can be triggered under appropriate parameter combinations, arising from the interplay of asymmetric coupling, medium memory and ratchet potential. Furthermore, under appropriate system parameters, noise can enhance the directed transport velocity, manifesting stochastic resonance in the system.

abstract: With the deep integration of digitalization and artificial intelligence technologies into enterprise knowledge management, AI-assisted learning is reshaping the channels through which knowledge is acquired within organizations. Meanwhile, knowledge dissemination is evolving from traditional interpersonal interaction toward human-machine collaborative interaction. In light of this transformation, this study develops a multi-stage 2SEIR-CA dynamic model of knowledge dissemination under an AI-enabled mechanism that incorporates dual-channel "interpersonal-human-machine" interaction. Specifically, employees are classified into five states: employees who have not yet mastered the knowledge, employees with limited knowledge mastery, employees with strong knowledge mastery, knowledge-disseminating employees, and knowledge-exited employees. On this basis, the next-generation matrix method is employed to calculate the basic reproduction number of the system and to analyze the existence and stability of equilibrium points. An optimal control model is then established to derive strategies for promoting knowledge dissemination, and a cellular automaton model is introduced to characterize its spatiotemporal evolution. The results show that the system exhibits a pronounced threshold effect: when key dissemination parameters exceed their critical levels, knowledge can continue to diffuse within the organization; otherwise, it will gradually decay. Second, the AI-enabled mechanism enhances knowledge transformation efficiency and contact intensity, thereby significantly promoting the transition of employees with strong knowledge mastery to knowledge-disseminating employees. Third, the optimal control strategy proposed in this study can optimize transformation pathways across different stages under resource constraints, thereby improving overall dissemination efficiency and maintaining the structural stability of the dissemination system. Fourth, the spatiotemporal simulations demonstrate that, under optimal regulation, knowledge dissemination can form a stable diffusion pattern with high coverage. Under the assumptions and parameter settings of the proposed model, the findings provide theoretical insights into the dynamic mechanisms underlying AI-enabled knowledge dissemination and offer model-based implications for knowledge management practices in organizations.

abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication of sepsis, significantly increasing both mortality risk and healthcare costs. Early prediction and diagnosis of sepsis-associated AKI (SA-AKI) remain challenging due to the delayed detection of existing renal injury markers. Although research suggests that the Renal Resistive Index (RRI) shows promise for earlier prediction of AKI, large-scale, multicenter clinical studies to support this are currently lacking. Methods This multicenter, open-label, prospective observational cohort study enrolled 238 patients who were diagnosed with sepsis according to the Sepsis 3.0 criteria. The Renal Resistive Index (RRI) was measured using bedside ultrasound within 2 hours of diagnosis and subsequently every 8 hours during their individualized standard treatment. Concurrently, blood samples were collected to quantify creatinine and cystatin C, and urine samples were obtained to detect kidney injury markers, including TIMP-2/IGFBP-7. The primary endpoint is to determine the threshold and accuracy of the Renal Resistive Index in predicting sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI). Secondary endpoints include examining the dynamic trend of the RRI, assessing the RRI's predictive value for 28-day mortality in sepsis, and evaluating the correlation between the RRI and creatinine, cystatin C, and urinary TIMP-2/IGFBP-7 levels. Discussion This study assesses the accuracy and feasibility of using bedside ultrasonography to monitor the Renal Resistive Index (RRI) for the early detection of sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI). Early identification of SA-AKI is crucial for improving clinical outcomes in sepsis, making this approach highly relevant for timely intervention. Ethics and dissemination This study received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the initiator's institution. Study results will be initially reported to the collaborating investigators. Following review and consensus by the Trial Steering Committee, the research report will be drafted by the initiating investigator and disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at scientific conferences. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400082420), Registered on March 28, 2024.
