title: Characterising sleep spindle emergence in infancy: Effects of prematurity and early locomotor intervention
abstract: Study objectives: Sleep spindles are thalamocortical oscillations evolving during early brain maturation. In adults, they support memory consolidation and are organised into rhythmic "trains" thought to support memory reactivation. How this temporal organisation emerges in infancy, and whether prematurity or early sensorimotor experience shapes it, remains unclear. This study characterised infant spindles and investigated how prematurity and early locomotor training affect their temporal and spatial organisation, providing insight into early brain maturation. Methods: Daytime high-density EEG sleep recordings were analysed in 50 infants born full-term (n=12) or very preterm (n=38, including 12 who received locomotor training) at 2 months corrected age. Spindle temporal organisation was analysed using a two-step Morlet wavelet transform to quantify slow modulations of spindle-band power (11-16Hz). Time-frequency decomposition around spindle onset was used to identify significant spindle-band scalp-wide activity, and topographical maps were statistically compared between groups. Results: All groups showed rhythmic spindle organisation, three times slower than in adults, with no group differences. Untrained preterm infants showed a more diffuse spindle-band activity than the distinct frontal and central clusters observed in full-term infants. Trained preterm infants exhibited a spatial distribution closely resembling that of full-term infants, although their frontal spindle density was lower than in both other groups. Conclusions: Spindle rhythmic organisation emerged early in infancy and remained unaffected by prematurity or locomotor training. Prematurity was associated with more diffuse spindle-band activity, suggesting reduced cortical specialisation, whereas trained preterm infants showed a spatial distribution resembling that of full-term infants, suggesting that early locomotor experience may influence thalamocortical organisation.

title: Walking Produces Oscillations in Orientation and Direction Perception at the Step Rate
abstract: Walking is one of the most stereotyped oscillatory movement able-bodied individuals produce. It is highly consistent within and across individuals, with people taking ~5000 steps a day on average at approximately 2 Hz. This consistency and its ubiquitous role in daily living make walking an ideal behaviour for investigating perception under active conditions. Across two virtual reality experiments, we tested whether stride-based oscillations, as seen in visual detection performance, also occur for visual orientation and motion direction discrimination. Participants followed a simulated screen along a linear path in virtual space while visual stimuli were presented on the screen. Group-level performance in both visual tasks oscillated at approximately two cycles per stride. Peak performance in visual orientation identification aligned with the late swing phase of each step, whereas peak performance in motion direction identification aligned with the late stance or early swing phase. These findings extend recent work showing that visual perception is modulated at the step rate during locomotion.

title: Joint reconstruction of multi-contrast relaxation-diffusion imaging
abstract: Diffusion MRI across multiple gradient directions, b-values and echo times (TEs) provides complementary tissue contrast but requires extensive sampling. Joint k-space and q-space undersampling requires reconstruction that preserves diffusion- and TE-dependent signal variation while exploiting shared anatomical information. Here we introduce DIFFUSE (Diffusion-relaxometry Implicit Field Fitting from Undersampled k-q Space across Echoes), a subject-specific joint k-q-TE image reconstruction framework. It fits a single implicit neural representation (INR) directly to complementary undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements across diffusion encodings and echo times. The INR (a self-supervised neural network) maps spatial location, b-value and TE to baseline b0 signals and spherical harmonic coefficients for directional diffusion-weighted image reconstruction. The measurement-specific forward model incorporates phase, coil sensitivities and motion and eddy current related transforms. We evaluated DIFFUSE using retrospective Human Connectome Project data, controlled motion simulations and in vivo multi-shell and multi-TE acquisitions. At sixfold in-plane acceleration, DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 57-73% relative to SENSE across two diffusion shells in the retrospective experiment. In the controlled motion experiment, motion-aware DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 66-72% relative to static DIFFUSE. The prospective study demonstrated multi-shell reconstruction at 1.3 mm isotropic resolution with significantly high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In a separate multi-TE experiment, a single representation jointly reconstructed all nine contrasts corresponding to 3 b-value/TE combinations. DIFFUSE thus provides a common reconstruction strategy for accelerated protocols spanning multiple diffusion encodings and echo times.

title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
abstract: Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
abstract: Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

title: Practical Identifiability of a Minimal Adaptive Learning-Gain Model for Binary Feedback: A Simulation Study
abstract: Social learning is jointly determined by several computationally distinct quantities, namely baseline belief (prior mean), sensitivity to feedback (learning gain), and the temporal uncertainty of belief (drift), which are rarely separated in empirical designs. Here we systematically characterise the practical identifiability and predictive adequacy of a minimal four-parameter adaptive learning-gain model of binary feedback: a latent belief v_t about the probability of a positive outcome is carried forward deterministically between observations while an internal confidence-precision state decays by a per-trial amount omega, and the belief is updated by a learning gain lambda from a deterministic prior mean mu with initial confidence precision sigma; sigma, omega and lambda are model-defined internal quantities, not validated psychological constructs. The simulated process is self-reinforcing: the same latent state both generates the binary outcome and represents the learner's belief, so the model does not represent inference about an independently evolving social environment. The study is therefore an analysis of a phenomenological adaptive filter under a specified binary stochastic process: its update equations are deliberately chosen rather than derived from the Bernoulli-logistic likelihood, and it does not reduce to a standard hierarchical Gaussian filter. Using fixed-seed simulation studies, we report four findings. First, joint maximum-likelihood recovery is poor. On the 24-condition parameter grid at T=80 (100 independent replications per condition), the belief mean mu shows comparatively smaller errors but is still not reliably recovered; sigma and omega show near-zero tolerance-based recovery that stays at most 0.002 across tolerance thresholds of 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 transformed units, whereas lambda recovery is low but not near-zero and increases with tolerance (0.078, 0.182 and 0.263 at tolerances 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0). Boundary convergence is strongest for sigma (upper bound) and omega (lower bound), whereas lambda boundary solutions are not uniform across grid conditions. In a separate single-parameter-vector experiment that varies trial length (T in {40, 80, 120, 240, 480}), extending the sequence alone does not repair recovery of the positive parameters, including lambda. Tolerance recovery concerns point estimates only; calibrated interval coverage is not evaluated and is not substituted by a flat profile or a boundary estimate. Second, profile-likelihood and trade-off diagnostics show flat likelihood regions for sigma and omega, with an asymmetric profile for lambda that constrains its upper range but is uninformative over its low range; the flat sigma-omega geometry replicates in a second, low-gain regime (a within-study replication, not a claim across the full condition grid), whereas the exact steepness of the lambda profile is regime-dependent. Three optimisers converge to the same boundary solution, and the fitted estimates cannot reliably rank individual simulated subjects either. These patterns support weak practical identifiability under the tested design, not structural non-identifiability; no formal structural identifiability analysis is performed, so a structural claim is not made. Third, a fitting-parity audit found and corrected a return-order defect in the fixed-gain candidate: its fitted parameters were returned with sigma and omega interchanged, which artificially raised that candidate's fitted block loss. Under the corrected fit, overall block discrimination is 67/150 = 0.45 under the original wider bounds and 72/150 = 0.48 under common fitting bounds matched to the proposed model (56 common forecast observations per dataset, each scored exactly once, with an automated index check confirming no fit-forecast overlap and no look-ahead), modestly above the 0.33 chance level; a calibrated permutation test that preserves the asymmetric winner marginals is significant (p = 0.0011 and p < 0.001). This above-chance accuracy is almost entirely attributable to Rescorla-Wagner (0.88-0.90 correct), whereas the adaptive filter and its nested fixed-gain restriction remain heavily confused (row-wise accuracies 0.18-0.22 and 0.24-0.36, neither significant), and the result is robust to the fitting bounds (row-wise p-values are descriptive and uncorrected; none of this establishes model equivalence). Fourth, across 50 independent held-out datasets the model shows no predictive advantage over a training-set empirical-frequency baseline (the paired 95% confidence interval spans zero under both normal-approximation and bootstrap estimation; the proportion of datasets won is not used as evidence of superiority), and a paired ablation shows no consistent predictive gain from the added update components and no improvement in parameter stability; no predictive advantage over this empirical-frequency baseline has therefore been demonstrated.

title: Encoding activity predicts distinct recognition signals during working and long-term memory in the human hippocampus
abstract: Neurocomputational models predict that episodic memories are represented by sparse, pattern-separated hippocampal codes. Recognition within working memory capacity may instead rely on overlapping cortical codes. We analyzed human intracranial microwire recordings during a continuous recognition task to test whether retrieval demand and spiking activity at encoding determine which neural signal is expressed. We show that relative increases in firing from pre-stimulus to post-stimulus onset at encoding predicted an item-specific signal that was present only in the hippocampus and only during long-term memory retrieval of remembered items. In contrast, consistently elevated firing predicted a generic signal that distinguished remembered from novel items, was present in the hippocampus during both working and long-term memory retrieval, and extended to the anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortices during working memory. These findings are consistent with a new theory that distinguishes working memory from long-term memory in terms of the neural coding scheme accessed at retrieval.

title: Covert attentional tracking with invisible phase tagging
abstract: Attention forms a fundamental component of visual processing. The locus and spread of covert attention reveals how specific locations or features in the environment are preferentially processed, however, tracking this process in a time-resolved fashion is not easy. Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) is a recent advance in localizing covert attention. This technique uses stimuli that flicker at unique frequencies to invisibly "tag" areas of the visual field. The frequency-specific response elicited offers a measure of visual processing (and covert attention) over time. However, the narrow frequency band compatible with RIFT restricts the number of distinct frequency tags that can be simultaneously used. This limitation can be addressed by using oscillatory phase as an additional tagging feature. Here, we conducted a RIFT-EEG experiment (n=24) with 8 unique tags based on both frequency and phase modulation. We show that modulations in visual processing can be measured at several tagged locations with identical frequency but different phases. This also allowed for the use of combined phase- and frequency- modulated RIFT to quantify the distribution of attention across the visual field. By integrating phase-modulation into invisible frequency tagging studies of attention, we bring the field a step closer towards fine-resolution attentional tracking continuously over time and space, allowing novel insights across various domains of visual cognition.

title: Self-enhancement and devaluation of others during belief formation are linked to narcissistic traits
abstract: Background: Narcissistic personality traits are associated with the tendency to maintain a grandiose self-image through self-enhancement and devaluation of others. Using computational modeling, we investigated how narcissistic traits and the experience of pride are linked to how individuals form beliefs about themselves and others. Methods: Healthy individuals and individuals with psychiatric diagnoses varying in narcissistic traits (N = 97) completed a learning task in which self-serving biases emerged implicitly through trial-by-trial belief updating in response to manipulated feedback. Computational modeling quantified how participants updated beliefs about their own and another person's abilities in response to better- and worse-than-expected performance feedback. Results: Higher narcissistic traits were associated with reduced learning from worse-than-expected self-related feedback, consistent with self-enhancement as a mechanism for maintaining a grandiose self-image. Individuals with higher narcissistic traits also reported greater pride following better-than-expected self-related feedback, which mediated the association between narcissistic traits and positive self-related learning. Furthermore, higher narcissistic traits were, mediated via pride, linked to increased learning from worse-than-expected feedback about the other person, suggesting that devaluing others relative to oneself may serve as a secondary pathway for maintaining a grandiose self-image. Discussion: These findings identify computational and affective mechanisms through which narcissistic traits are linked to self- and other-related belief formation. Reduced integration of negative self-related feedback together with enhanced pride following positive feedback may support grandiose self-beliefs, while enhanced learning from negative information about others suggests that individuals with higher narcissistic traits implicitly construct themselves as superior through both self-enhancement and devaluation of others during interpersonal belief formation.

title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
abstract: Background: Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Methods: Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n=35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n=38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n=63). Classification-relevant subnetwork nodal strength was associated post hoc with trait impulsivity within P+ groups. Results: P+CSO- were significantly distinguished from P-CSO- (balanced accuracy [BAC]=0.621, pFDR=.041), and showed reductions between default-mode hubs and temporoparietal somatomotor and ventral attention regions. P+CSO+ were also significantly distinguished from P+CSO- (BAC=0.645, pFDR=.032) and yielded a smaller subnetwork centered on the substantia nigra. Against P-CSO-, P+CSO+ showed widespread reductions, particularly across subcortical, default mode, visual, limbic, and somatomotor regions (BAC=0.640, pFDR=0.032). Right precentral gyrus nodal strength correlated with impulsivity in P+CSO+ only (r=0.57, pFDR=0.024). Conclusions: Whole-brain rsFC contains information distinguishing pedohebephilic preference in the absence of known CSO, while P+CSO+ show additional and more widespread network alterations involving systems implicated in action selection and behavioral regulation. These findings open new avenues for integrating pedohebephilia into broader neurobiological research frameworks.

title: Heavy-tailed connections support robust neural communication
abstract: In the synaptic wiring between neurons, some rare connections are orders of magnitude stronger than most. This heavy-tailed connectivity is ubiquitous across different species, brain regions, and cell types, suggesting that it serves a general purpose for neural function. Here, we show, both analytically and in simulations, that heavy-tailed connections reduce communication errors in the presence of synaptic noise. In minimal models of individual neurons, noisy connections induce errors at a rate that depends only on a simple network statistic, which we refer to as robustness. For a fixed number of incoming synapses, neurons with broader distributions of connection strength are more robust and, therefore, admit fewer errors. Across several connectomes, we find that real neurons are consistently more robust than comparable null networks. In the whole brain of the fruit fly Drosophila, robustness increases with distance from the sensory periphery, such that central neurons are more robust than those involved in sensory processing. Together, these results indicate that heavy-tailed connections may arise universally to fortify the brain against noise in communication.

title: Somatotopic Organization of the Ventroposterior Nucleus of the Thalamus in Macaque Monkeys with Dorsal Spinal Cord Injuries Sustained During Early Postnatal Development
abstract: Injuries to peripheral nerves or the spinal cord lead to changes in the topographic organization in the brain at multiple levels along the sensory pathways. In adult monkeys large-scale deafferentations due to transection of the dorsal columns of the spinal cord at cervical levels result in large-scale reorganizations such that the deafferented neurons in the hand representation of somatosensory cortical area 3b start responding to anatomically distant body parts such as the chin. However, reorganization following dorsal column injuries depends upon the age at the time of the injury. The somatotopy of areas 3b, 1 and 2 in macaque monkeys with injuries sustained on or before postnatal day (PND) 5 is very normal-like. Whereas in monkeys with injuries sustained between PND9 and PND12, a large extent of the deafferented somatosensory cortex remains unresponsive to peripheral touch, with neurons at only a few sites responding to touch on the face or arm. Here we determined the organization of the ventroposterior nucleus (VPN) of the thalamus in four of these monkeys (Macaca radiata, 3 females, 1 male) that received lesions of the dorsal columns on PND 3, 5 and 9. We show that the nature of reorganization of VPN largely resembles that of the somatosensory cortex. Somatotopy is normal-like after lesions on PND3 and 5, whereas after lesion on PND9, the deprived neurons are largely unresponsive to peripheral touch, with a limited expansion of the chin representation.

title: The insect brain is specified by a conserved transcriptional program distinct from the segmental CNS
abstract: The brain is the central processing center that integrates information to guide animal behavior, while the posterior CNS performs less central functions. To what degree this functional distinction is reflected in divergence of the genetic regulation remains unexplored, as well as the hypothesis of a distinct evolutionary origin of brain and trunk CNS. In insects, neuroblast biology is similar across the CNS, but the presence of brain-specific neuroblast types and differences in the gene sets involved in their spatial and temporal specification indicate divergence. However, a comprehensive and unbiased comparison of the regulatory code of brain versus trunk neuroblasts has been lacking. Here, we reveal the transcription factors expressed in insect embryonic neuroblasts by a combined single-cell analysis from the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the beetle Tribolium castaneum, for which we established a Gal4 enhancer trap system to generate a line marking NBs with tGFP. From the combined dataset of nearly 70,000 neuroblasts, we identified around 23,000 brain neuroblasts, from which we identified cell populations and their transcriptional signatures. We found 188 brain-specific TFs, including seven spatially restricted transcription factors not previously associated with neuroblasts (Hmx, CG15696, CG32532, dmrt99B, fD59A, TfAP-2, and Fer1). In addition to the expected canonical Type II NBs, we found two related clusters with intriguing transcriptional divergence. The large number of brain-specific TFs supports a profound divergence between the insect brain and posterior CNS. Together with recent work in vertebrates, our data confirm an ancient divergence of the brain from the trunk.

title: PhaseICA: Resolving Individual-Specific Macroscale Brain Propagations
abstract: Understanding complex dynamics from spatiotemporal signals requires robust tools capable of decoding reoccurring patterns. Traditional ICA methods often overlook the spatially non-stationarity nature of brain activity across both the frequency and spatial domains. We propose a novel data-driven approach, named PhaseICA, designed to extract reoccurring spatiotemporal patterns, referred to as brain waves. Unlike conventional ICA methods that focus solely on amplitude, PhaseICA incorporates phase information directly into the component estimation, preserving the nonstationary property that real-valued ICA methods typically discard. The method performs spatial independence optimization in the complex domain by minimizing a complex entropy bound over the eigenvectors of Hilbert-transformed signals. The proposed method captures spatial propagation across brain regions with interpretable and compact representations, offering a promising foundation for decoding brain dynamic systems and revealing the temporal relationship of regions.

title: The marginal brain
abstract: Goal-directed cognition raises brain energy use only a few percent above resting use, a figure often read as evidence that cognition is metabolically cheap. Models of endogenous precision derive the precision of neural representations from a cost on encoding activity whose unit price is a free parameter. Embedding endogenous precision in a regulated, shared energy budget makes this cost the shadow price of energy at the margin of the budget. Neither the task share of the budget nor the net whole-brain increment identifies this price; when tasks face a common price ratio and coding technology is stable, imprecision changes by the exact fourth root of that ratio, so that the cost of information rescales while its shape is preserved; and the co-movement of imprecision and stimulus-linked task energy separates price changes from changes in coding technology. In 12,960 published estimation trials, response variance at matched numerosities rises with prior width in line with the ratios that the calibrated model predicts out of sample, and simulations indicate that a doubled price is detectable with existing paradigms when state-dependent lapses are modeled.

title: Dual reinforcement-learning network modules for modeling decision-making with multiple strategies
abstract: Animals and humans use multiple behavioral strategies to perform tasks. However, neural implementations of multiple strategies remain elusive, as some studies propose distinct pathways, while others observe overlapping brain regions associated with strategies. We propose a hybrid deep reinforcement learning (H-DRL) method, in which one network model implements model-free and inference-based behaviors through synaptic plasticity and recurrent activity. H-DRL uses a single updating rule and switches the strategy according to task demands without an explicit arbitrator. H-DRL reproduced mixed strategies of humans in a two-step task. In the mouse perceptual decision-making task, H-DRL adapted the recurrent dynamics with rich learning when the task condition required inference-based behavior, while adopting model-free behavior with lazy learning for a simple condition. The activity of H-DRL units showed condition-dependent maintenance of previous events, consistent with orbitofrontal cortical activity in mice. Our model provides a unified view that one cortical network automatically determines strategies in use depending on task conditions.

title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
abstract: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.

title: Mesoscale Functional Reorganization of Cortical Networks After Cortical Spreading Depression
abstract: Background: Resting-state functional imaging is increasingly used to understand how cortical networks modulate and respond to pain. Awake imaging with a minimally invasive approach is key to observe the natural state of the brain. As migraine with aura, a common headache disorder, can be experimentally modeled by cortical spreading depressions (CSD) in rodents, it is essential to understand the impact of CSD on functional connectivity and network topology to find imaging cues of trigeminovascular activation and headache. Methods: We used awake widefield intrinsic optical-signal imaging (IOSI) on optically cleared windows to non-invasively characterize the impact of CSDs on bihemispheric resting-state static and dynamic functional connectivity patterns and network topology. A subset of mice was chronically treated with amitriptyline to examine the effect of susceptibility to CSD on connectivity. After baseline imaging, CSD was triggered optogenetically and confirmed by laser speckle contrast imaging. A group of mice received intraperitoneal naproxen after CSD to suppress headache. IOSI was repeated at 30 minutes, 60 minutes, 4 hours, and 24 hours after CSD. The mouse grimace scale was scored at each time point for behavioral headache documentation. Results: We observed time-dependent changes in resting-state functional connectivity that were reversed by naproxen. Amitriptyline, a prophylactic migraine medication, decreased susceptibility to CSD and modified resting-state functional connectivity differently than controls. Network analysis with graph-theoretical methods revealed barrel and retrosplenial cortices as potential key players in trigeminal pain processing after CSD. Dynamic functional connectivity analysis demonstrated functional connectivity states, with fractional occupancy and mean dwell time of these states showing distinct CSD and pain-modulated states. A support vector machine was utilized to predict CSD-mediated dynamic connectivity changes in controls. Conclusion: Our results bring insight into potentially headache-associated changes in resting-state cortical functional connectivity after CSD and how this functional reorganization is influenced by acute and chronic medications for migraine.

title: Improving DASH adherence after midlife promotes better late-life cognition and brain health: the SG70 Study
abstract: Healthier dietary patterns reduce cognitive impairment risks, but whether diet improvement after mid-life can benefit cognition and brain health, and how brain measures mediate diet-cognition associations, remain unclear, as few studies had long-term diet records alongside detailed neuroimaging and cognitive measures. We assessed adherence to the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) in 892 SG70 participants, nested within the Singapore Chinese Health Study, between 1993-2025. Adherence during midlife (44-55 years) and early elderhood (61-73 years) were related to seven cognitive domains, brain morphometry, white matter hyperintensities (WMH), and free-water markers measured in late life (68-82 years). Higher adherence at both mid-life stages was associated with better verbal memory. Higher mid-life adherence was associated with greater white matter volume in association tracts, whereas higher early-elderhood adherence was associated with lower free water (frontal and occipital) and lower WMH (basal ganglia and anterior periventricular). Moreover, white matter volume and free water mediated the diet-verbal memory associations at their respective midlife stages. Importantly, participants with improved mid-to-late life diet trajectories showed better late-life verbal memory and brain health than those with persistently low adherence. Overall, ensuring mid-life diet quality and improving post-midlife diet may promote cognitive resilience through structural reserve and neurovascular health.

title: Memory-based and surround-based pattern completion show distinct laminar profiles in human V1
abstract: Visual input is often incomplete, requiring the brain to infer missing information from prior experience or contextual cues. Establishing whether memory-derived and context-derived information shape pattern completion through shared or distinct top-down pathways is central to understanding how perception emerges from the integration of sensory input and prior knowledge. Across two experiments, we used 7T layer fMRI to measure activity in an occluded region of human V1 while participants viewed natural scenes. Memory-based completion was enabled by varying the level of exposure to full scene images before scanning, while surround-based completion was implemented via two scenes that were repeatedly presented in partially occluded form but never seen intact. In both fMRI experiments, category decoding in the occluded V1 region only emerged after multiple prior exposures, whereas novel scenes did not show reliable decoding. Repeated partially occluded scenes also supported decoding, despite the hidden region never being shown, consistent with surround-based pattern completion. Critically, mnemonic and surround-based pattern completion showed opposite laminar decoding profiles across V1 depths, with mnemonic feedback dominating deep layers, and surround-based feedback dominating superficial layers. Together, these findings suggest that completion in the early visual cortex depends on the sources of inferred information, revealing dissociable feedback pathways for memory- and context-driven inference.

title: Inferring brain structural complexity from dynamical measures
abstract: Complexity, commonly defined as the coexistence of integration and differentiation, is a fundamental property of thalamocortical networks and is regarded as a prerequisite for adaptive brain function and consciousness. A variety of metrics have been developed to estimate neural complexity from recorded activity and are increasingly employed in both research and clinical settings. Yet, the extent to which these measures reflect specific architectural features of the underlying circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we used Wilson-Cowan mean-field equations to simulate neural dynamics across networks spanning a broad range of architectures. By systematically rewiring connectivity, we generated graded variations in the structural integration-differentiation balance and assessed a panel of complexity measures derived either from spontaneous activity (observational metrics) or from responses to external perturbations (perturbational metrics). Observational measures exhibited markedly heterogeneous behavior: some were primarily sensitive to network integration, others to differentiation, whereas some showed limited sensitivity to architectural manipulations. In contrast, perturbational measures robustly peaked at intermediate rewiring steps and scaled with small-worldness, consistent with architectures that combine local recurrence and distributed communication. Moreover, perturbational metrics proved robust to common-driver confounds and were highest in a wake-like regime near critical instability, declining as sleep-like dynamics became more widespread across the network. Taken together, these findings map widely used empirical complexity measures onto specific network architectures, reveal dynamical factors that can bias observational estimates, and provide guidance for inferring complexity in systems whose internal organization is inaccessible, unconventional, or only partially known, including brain organoids, non-human nervous systems, and synthetic neural networks.

title: Similarity in greater Chinese ideology is associated with intersubject neural similarity during viewing of a pro-China video
abstract: When people watch the same political narrative, they often form different interpretations. Although prior research has shown that political ideology can shape shared neural responses to sociopolitical content, less is known about how individual differences in national identity ideology are associated with inter-individual similarity in neural dynamics during naturalistic viewing, particularly in sociopolitical contexts where national identity is highly salient in public discourse. We examined Greater Chinese ideology, one dimension of national identity ideology, in relation to positive engagement and neural dynamics during viewing of the same pro-China video across two samples in Taiwan. In Study 1 (N = 52), higher Greater Chinese ideology was associated with greater positive engagement. In Study 2 (N = 60), participants underwent fMRI while viewing the same video. Intersubject representational similarity analysis showed that greater similarity in participants' Greater Chinese ideology item-response profiles was associated with greater similarity in neural dynamics in regions associated with the frontoparietal control, salience, and default mode networks. Notably, the within-versus-between neural similarity effect was stronger among participants with relatively lower Greater Chinese ideology scores than among those with relatively higher scores. These findings link Greater Chinese ideology to positive engagement and similarity in neural dynamics during viewing of this pro-China video. Further research is needed to determine whether similar associations can be observed across other dimensions of national identity ideology and different political narratives.

title: Characterization of Fetal Cortical Development Using Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY)
abstract: The prenatal period of human brain development is critical for mental health and cognition across the entire lifespan. During this period, the cortex undergoes a dramatic transformation from a smooth lissencephalic surface into an elaborately folded structure, a process whose precise characterization is essential for understanding neurodevelopmental trajectories. This study represents the first application of Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY) to a large multi-centric fetal brain MRI dataset (635 subjects, 20-38 weeks gestational age). SPANGY characterizes geometric variations on a surface based on the wavelength of folds, hence, providing a quantitative local description of gyrification at the individual level. Using rigorous normative modeling (GAMLSS) and statistical harmonization (ComBat-GAM), we established age-specific reference trajectories for multi-scale gyrification features (spectral frequency bands). We provide the first ever quantification of the temporally-ordered emergence of cortical folding in successive waves during the entire second half of pregnancy: the earliest-emerging low frequency, deep fissures are progressively superseded by the accelerating expansion of higher frequency folds. The normative curves provide the first step in taking prenatal neurodevelopmental assessment from qualitative inspection into a rigorous statistical inference, creating an objective reference against which deviations from healthy brain growth could be caught earlier.

title: Role of leg campaniform sensilla proprioceptive feedback in Drosophila melanogaster adaptive walking
abstract: With the newly uncovered access to a genetic line labeling all campaniform sensilla in Drosophila melanogaster and the many insights gathered from larger insects, we analyzed the distribution and patterning of this class of proprioceptors throughout the fly nervous system and studied CS function in motor control. We demonstrate via two-photon calcium imaging microscopy that campaniform sensilla activation induces activity in many leg muscles, showing that these proprioceptive stimuli can influence motor neuron activity. We then dissected how the lack of these proprioceptive stimuli influence walking behavior, leg kinematics, and interleg coordination in freely-walking flies using transient optogenetic inhibition and video tracking with high spatiotemporal resolution. We show that campaniform sensilla inhibition robustly affects Drosophila melanogasters ability to reach their typical walking speeds. Detailed analysis of leg kinematic suggests that shorter stance amplitudes characterized by their long-lasting duration were behind the speed deficits. Dissecting this phenotype also revealed the inability to maintain coordinated interleg stepping patterns as well as postural control in absence of proprioceptive force and load feedback.

title: Neuron types and distribution of a Drosophila driver line collection
abstract: Cell type designations label uniquely-identifiable groups of related cells that typically function in similar ways. Cell types divide the Drosophila melanogaster central nervous system into functional units, but remain challenging to target and identify. Previously we generated a driver line and image resource for targeting many neuron types (Meissner et al., 2025). Here we improve on identifying the targeted neurons by automated searching against electron microscopy datasets and manual scoring of search results to add 6,368 annotations across 1,772 driver lines in the collection. These annotations provide a potential training resource for future search algorithms. We then estimate the number of cell types and thus the fraction of the central nervous system labeled by the collection as a whole.

title: Rare mutations implicate CGE interneurons as a vulnerable axis of cognitive deficits across psychiatric disorders
abstract: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia (SCZ) share genetic risk factors, including rare high penetrance single nucleotide variants and copy number variants (CNVs), and exhibit both overlapping and distinct clinical phenotypes. Cognitive deficits and intellectual disability-critical predictors of long-term outcomes-are common to both conditions. To investigate shared and disorder-specific neurobiological impact of highly penetrant rare mutations in ASD and SCZ, we analyzed human single-nucleus whole-brain sequencing data to identify strongly affected brain cell types. Our analysis revealed Caudal Ganglionic Eminence (CGE)-derived GABAergic interneurons as a critical nexus for cognitive deficits across these disorders. Notably, genes within 22q11.2 deletions, known to confer a high risk of SCZ, ASD, and cognitive impairment, showed a strong expression bias toward vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing cells (VIP+) among CGE subtypes. To explore VIP+ GABAergic interneuron perturbations in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in vivo, we examined their activity in the Df(16)A+/- mouse model during a spatial navigation task and observed reduced activity along with altered responses to random rewards. At the population level, VIP+ interneurons exhibited impaired spatial encoding and diminished subtype-specific activity suggesting deficient disinhibition in CA1 microcircuits in the hippocampus, a region essential for learning and memory. Overall, these results demonstrate the crucial role of CGE-derived interneurons in mediating cognitive processes that are disrupted across a range of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Hierarchical connectivity sets the upper critical dimension of neural avalanches
abstract: Neural avalanches with size exponent $3/2$ are usually explained by mean-field critical branching, which for short-range coupling requires dimension $N\ge4$. We show that hierarchical connectivity removes this constraint. In a $p$-adic version of the Buice--Cowan field theory, a coupling that decays by $p^{-(N+σ)}$ per hierarchical level selects the Taibleson--Vladimirov operator, and the critical theory is ultrametric directed percolation with upper critical dimension $N_c=2σ$. Exact simulations on a tree give $τ_S=3/2$ for $σ\le N/2$, decreasing continuously for $σ>N/2$.

title: p-Adic statistical field theory of fluctuation effects in hierarchical neural networks
abstract: The Buice-Cowan field theory [PRE 75, 051919 (2007)] describes fluctuations and correlations of neural activity through a path integral whose mean-field limit is the Wilson-Cowan equation and whose critical behavior belongs to the directed percolation class. In its continuum limit the neurons are the points of a Euclidean space and activity spreads by ordinary diffusion, which encodes neither the hierarchical organization of cortical networks nor their small-world property. We formulate a version of the theory in which the neurons are organized in an infinite, self-similar, tree-like structure, described by the p-adic numbers. The path integral carries over unchanged, and finite networks are exact restrictions of the continuum theory. The main change is in the linear response: in the Euclidean theory every short-range kernel reduces to the Laplacian, while in the p-adic theory each connectivity kernel gives its own nonlocal p-adic diffusion operator. For couplings that decay by a fixed factor per level of the hierarchy this is the Taibleson-Vladimirov operator, and the critical theory is an ultrametric Reggeon field theory whose upper critical dimension is twice the decay exponent of the coupling. Hence the decay of the coupling up the hierarchy, and not the dimension of space, decides whether mean-field exponents apply. We obtain a Ginzburg-type criterion, loop-corrected hierarchical Wilson-Cowan equations, log-periodic corrections to scaling and power-law correlations. Exact simulations on a tree support the predictions: the avalanche-size exponent takes the mean-field value 3/2 when the coupling decays slowly and decreases toward the directed-percolation value when it decays fast. The hierarchical network is also small-world when the decay exponent is smaller than the dimension, a property that the Euclidean theory obtains only by assuming long-range coupling.

title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

title: Temporal smoothness constraints on efficient neurobiological codes imply temporal specialization
abstract: Neurobiological circuits may be energy efficient in part because there is a division of labor: different subsystems compute or represent different things. In light of this, it is interesting that a major difference between subsystems is the time scale on which they typically vary. Here, we argue that temporal smoothness constraints---the idea that it may be energetically costly for systems to vary much more quickly than their typical time scale---imply a certain division of labor with respect to temporal stimulus features. In particular, slow subsystems ought to represent slowly varying stimulus features, and fast subsystems ought to represent quickly varying features. We formulate a novel efficient coding model that we use to investigate this claim, and exactly solve for the optimal division of labor. In addition to finding that slower subsystems ought to represent more slowly varying temporal features, we find surprising structure of mathematical interest: optimal codes have subsystems which represent orthogonal temporal features, and which correspond to the eigenfunctions of a Sturm-Liouville problem.

title: MtReNIRS: A Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Transferable Neurovascular Representations
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a promising approach for monitoring the hemodynamic correlates of neural activity in naturalistic settings. However, existing modeling methods for fNIRS are largely confined to small-scale, single-session data with low sampling rates, driven by high heterogeneity in acquisition devices and optode montages. In addition, the complex spatiotemporal structure of fNIRS signals further restricts model scalability and transferability across settings. As a result, it remains unclear whether a single fNIRS encoder can learn representations that are usable across subjects, tasks, devices, and montages. Here, we show that a montage-aware masked autoencoder, pretrained on 12 public fNIRS datasets spanning 268 subjects and 567 recording hours, learns generalizable neurovascular representations that transfer across three external datasets. Our fNIRS foundation model, MtReNIRS, jointly encodes the slow hemodynamic nature of fNIRS, chromophore identity and cortical location by mapping heterogeneous montages onto a shared anatomical reference. MtReNIRS achieves cross-subject performance on par or better than fully supervised baselines and excels in few-shot within-subject calibration, where it outperforms prior state-of-the-art fNIRS models, while remaining robust to sparse montages. Our results indicate that montage-aware self-supervision yields physiologically grounded, transferable fNIRS representations, providing a scalable foundation for label-efficient brain-computer interfaces.

title: On the stability of learning
abstract: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true---learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

title: A theory of noisy linear recurrent neural network learning dynamics
abstract: Biological neural networks are noisy: their dynamics involve difficult-to-predict fluctuations which are likely due not just to chaos, but also to a variety of low-level biophysical processes. Despite the omnipresence of intrinsic noise, its theoretical consequences are incompletely understood, especially in the context of learning. For example, does noise meaningfully shape representation learning, or is it better viewed as a nuisance factor whose presence or absence changes little about what solution is found and when? Here, we argue that intrinsic noise can significantly modulate representation learning in recurrent neural networks (RNNs), since it can strongly break solution-space degeneracies and in some cases control whether a non-degenerate solution exists at all. We show that this is true for an analytically tractable model of noisy RNN learning with a linear activation function and white noise inputs. We find that, in the so-called rich regime (where weights are initialized with small values), noise strongly modulates the directions in which the read-in, readout, and recurrent weights align. Moreover, we find that noise produces a kind of phase transition: for sufficiently high noise, a non-degenerate solution is not even optimal if parameter scales are limited (e.g., via regularization). These results extend recent analytic work on RNN representation learning and show that noise can act as a fundamental determinant of representations.

title: Phase response approach to networked neural activity models with delays
abstract: Networks of delay-coupled neural mass models alternate between synchrony and anti-phase locking as the delay between brain regions increases. The origin of these delay-dependent bands has remained unclear. Here, we show that a single function, the phase interaction function $H$ of an isolated node, predicts where the bands occur and explains why they repeat. For a Wilson--Cowan model with intra-nodal delay $τ$ and inter-nodal delay $ρ$, we compute the limit cycle and phase response, and hence $H$, by harmonic balance. Each band boundary is a zero of $H'$ shifted by the phase lag $Ωρ$, so the bands repeat in $ρ$ with the oscillation period. Simulations of the full delay-differential networks confirm these predictions, from two nodes, where predicted frequencies agree to second order in the coupling strength, to rings, where the theory also identifies coexisting stable twisted states that random initial conditions rarely reach. At weak coupling, the delays at which synchrony gains or loses stability are set by the node dynamics alone, whereas stable anti-phase states require a bipartite network. For a macaque connectome, metastability peaks at the edges of the synchrony bands, where the stability margin of phase-locking vanishes. The reduction is accurate for coupling strengths well below the slowest Floquet exponent of the node, beyond which a phase--amplitude description is needed. More broadly, vanishing phase-locking stability provides a simple route to metastability in delay-coupled oscillator networks and a candidate mechanism for the flexible coordination of brain dynamics.

title: Comparing Measurements of Pictorial Depth: Conditions for Placing Methods, Observers and Depiction Styles on One Scale
abstract: Two observers can agree about what lies in front in a picture yet report different amounts of apparent depth. People report pictorial depth by judging which of two points looks nearer, setting a probe to match a surface, adjusting relative sizes, or rating three-dimensionality. Two such methods can agree closely without sharing a unit. We ask when different methods, observers, depiction styles and viewing conditions can share one scale. Each set of scores, a measurement block, is a graph node. Two blocks are linked only if their shared observations pass six checks fixed in advance, among them outcome type, removal of declared offsets and position effects, proportionality and covariance. If the adjusted shared patterns are exactly proportional, a connected graph fixes every block's gain, its relative scale factor. The checks accept proportionality only within a set margin, so a link supports the gains without proving exact proportionality. One unit is still not one depth coordinate. Suppose each block scores shared stimuli with its own origin and positive unit. A matrix-rank test then decides when a common coordinate is identified: when only one overall origin and unit remain free. If each shared stimulus, an anchor, is scored by exactly two blocks, this needs two disjoint sets of anchors, each connecting every block, their compatibility assumed, not tested. They also suffice, except for anchor values satisfying exact polynomial relations (probability zero for anchor values drawn from any distribution with a density). We adapt network gain estimation from test linking, with a loop-consistency check. A reanalysis of published probe settings on 3-D renderings passes one of 171 candidate depiction-style links through all six checks, each judged by its own 95% bound, unadjusted for the 171 pairs. Links between tasks remain untested; they need shared stimuli and a joint uncertainty model.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Parkinson's Disease Classification from Resting-State Functional Connectivity
abstract: Altered resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is a candidate marker for the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Publicly available PD datasets, however, are small and fragmented across sites, scanners and clinical criteria. Transfer learning mitigates data scarcity by reusing a model trained on larger cohorts, but represents their knowledge primarily through a single set of weights shared by all individuals. Motivated by precision neuroimaging, we propose a retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) framework that additionally places each target individual in the context of similar individuals from external cohorts. A graph convolutional autoencoder (GAE), trained on external PD and control cohorts, encodes these cohorts into a neuro-knowledge base. Each target individual is encoded using the pretrained GAE, and its nearest neighbors are retrieved from the external knowledge base. Their embeddings are combined with the target embedding using mean aggregation or attention for classification. A systematic comparison on the TaoWu cohort separated the contributions of encoder pretraining, retrieval, attention and partial fine-tuning. Pretraining improved mean classification accuracy from 60.5% to 66.0%. However, retrieval and attention did not consistently improve performance over the pretrained-only variants. Several retrieval-based configurations nevertheless showed modestly higher ROC-AUC than the randomly initialized baseline. Varying the number of retrieved neighbors and partially fine-tuning the encoder provided no consistent additional gains. Retrieval-neighborhood analysis further showed diagnostically mixed neighborhoods. These findings provide initial evidence that population-learned representations can be complemented by individual-specific retrieval in neuroimaging, although larger datasets are needed to determine when such contextual information improves classification.

title: Regional prediction of hematoma expansion from non-contrast computed tomography in spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage patients
abstract: Background The combination of hematoma location, expansion and final volume influence neurological outcome. The aim of this study was to derive and validate a quantitative and interpretable region-based NCCT image feature model for predicting hematoma expansion. Methods The Ethnic/Racial Variations of Intracerebral Hemorrhage(ERICH) study was used for derivation and the Virtual International Trials in Stroke Archive(VISTA) was used for validation. NCCT images at presentation and 24+/-6hours were pre-processed, segmented and categorized into lobar, basal ganglia or thalamic regions. Hematoma expansion was defined by region and according to its effect on clinical outcome. Transport-based morphometry (TBM) produced a unique transport-based representation from each NCCT hematoma image. Linear classifiers applied to transport representations were used to derive a predictive model. The regional TBM model's performance was compared to alternate methods using AUROC analyses. Results The derivation dataset included 574 patients, comprising 162 lobar, 257 basal ganglia and 155 thalamic hematomas. The validation dataset included 196 patients, comprising 31 lobar, 119 basal ganglia and 46 thalamic hematomas. A combined regional model predicted hematoma expansion in the validation dataset with an AUROC of 0.787. The principal image features which varied by location were size, heterogeneity, eccentricity and density distribution towards the hematoma periphery. The regional TBM model outperformed alternative clinician based and machine-learning methods. Conclusions TBM discriminated and visualized regional features of hematoma expansion from presentation NCCT scans. This provides preliminary evidence for regional radiographic features of hematoma expansion. It has the potential to improve hematoma expansion prediction and understanding of hematoma expansion pathophysiology.

title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.

title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

title: Dynamic heart rate variability for classification of arrhythmia burden
abstract: Purpose: Heart rate variability (HRV) may provide information beyond heart rate (HR) for identifying arrhythmia burden, but the value of temporal HRV variation remains unclear. This study developed a dynamic HRV measure quantifying the interquartile range of window-level root mean square of successive RR-interval differences (IQRRMSSD) and evaluated its utility in classifying total abnormal-beat and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden compared with the conventional RR-based HRV measure, RMSSD. Methods: Manually annotated 30-minute ECG recordings from 43 individuals were analyzed using overlapping windows. A linear support vector classifier was used to classify individuals as having high or low arrhythmia burden, defined using 1% and 10% burden thresholds. Four feature sets were evaluated: HR alone, HR with RMSSD, HR with IQRRMSSD, and all three measures. Performance was assessed using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Results: HRV-containing feature sets generally outperformed HR alone, depending on outcome and threshold. At the 1% threshold, IQRRMSSD showed particularly high sensitivity for total abnormal-beat and PVC burden ($0.970 \pm 0.064$ and $0.882 \pm 0.193$, respectively). At the 10% threshold, conventional RMSSD showed the strongest overall discrimination, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.947 for PVC burden. Combined features sometimes improved the sensitivity-specificity balance but not overall discrimination. Conclusion: These findings suggest that a conventional RR-based HRV measure is informative for elevated ectopic burden, while a dynamic HRV measure may provide complementary information for lower-burden abnormalities.

title: Multiscale MIGHT: Modeling Local and Systemic Particle Transport in the Cardiovascular System
abstract: Analytical models of signaling molecule (SM) transport in the cardiovascular system (CVS) force a choice between whole-body scope and vessel-level resolution: Pharmacokinetic models for systemic transport lump each organ and lack small-scale structure, whereas synthetic molecular communication (MC) channel models resolve branched vessel networks (VNs) only for a single pass or capture recirculation only in topologically simple loops, and only partially include SM degradation. To close this gap, we propose Multiscale MIGHT, an extension of the Mixture of Inverse Gaussians for Hemodynamic Transport (MIGHT) model that jointly captures branched topologies, closed-loop circulation, organ clearance, and chemical degradation of SMs. First, we connect the ends of a branched VN to form a closed loop with local and global SM degradation, model the closed-loop channel impulse response for arbitrary transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) positions as a Laplace-domain feedback system, and approximate it in closed form by an inverse Gaussian mixture over multi-pass trajectories. The model is validated against finite-element simulations in COMSOL. Second, we set up a whole-body model, where an exemplary local VN, resolved at vessel-level detail, is embedded into the remaining systemic circulation, represented by lumped organ blocks. We simulate whole-body SM transport for various Tx sites and SM species. Our results show that, at an Rx in a local VN, only the initial pass produces a distinct peak in the SM concentration, significantly shaped by the local vasculature in case of small Tx-Rx distances; subsequent passes arrive strongly dispersed and are shaped almost entirely by organ clearance and chemical degradation rather than by the local VN topology.
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures; Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027

title: Escaping cells dilute CRISPR screen responses unequally across cell types
abstract: Single-cell CRISPR screens run in many cell types are used to compare how cell types respond to perturbation, to train models that transfer effects between them and to score such models. These uses assume that cells carrying a guide RNA had their target knocked down. Yet cells grow for days before sequencing: when an essential gene is knocked down, knocked-down cells are depleted or stop dividing while cells that escaped knockdown keep growing, and the measured response, an average over all cells carrying the guide, is diluted. We define the escape fraction of a perturbation as the share of its measured cells whose target was not effectively knocked down, and estimate it from each cell's counts of the targeted gene with a two-group mixture that recovers known fractions in simulated mixtures. In most cell types the escape fraction rises with how essential the gene is, it is higher in a later screen of the same cells, and it reaches about half of the measured cells in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). It predicts how much each response is diluted: the response size falls to (1 - e)^2 of that of the knocked-down cells. Because the escape fraction differs between cell types, it changes all three uses: hESCs respond like K562 cells unless knockdown depletes them, the coefficient a simple transfer model learns is lowered by the dilution of the cell type it predicts, and a benchmark scored on all cells rewards predictions shrunk towards no change, partly because that ground truth is itself diluted. Where cells stop dividing instead, the response also contains expression differences between cell-cycle stages. Response sizes should be compared on knocked-down cells or corrected for the escape fraction.
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary Information and data files are included as ancillary files. Code: https://github.com/xuanruihuang/which-cells-are-measured

title: Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival Inference for EHR Association Studies With Limited Chart Review
abstract: Objective: To reduce bias and improve precision in survival association studies using electronic health record (EHR) data when computational phenotypes (CPs) for outcomes and covariates are error-prone and chart review is limited. Materials and Methods: We developed Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival (MAPS) regression, which combines chart-reviewed and CP-derived labels across different validation patterns. MAPS uses a discrete-time survival model with a complementary log-log link to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). It incorporates data-adaptive augmentation weights, inverse-probability sampling weights, and patient-level cluster-robust variance estimation. We compared MAPS with chart-reviewed data (CRD) and CP-only analyses in simulation studies and a masked-validation study of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) among 1,026 patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Results: In the main simulations, MAPS produced approximately unbiased estimates and generally near-nominal 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, with narrower intervals than CRD. CP-only estimates became increasingly biased as CP errors increased. In the EHR analysis, MAPS estimates closely agreed with fully validated estimates and improved precision over CRD, particularly at lower validation rates. CP-only analysis suggested increased irAE risk associated with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID; HR=1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.09), whereas the fully validated analysis did not (HR=0.93; 95% CI, 0.67-1.29). Discussion: Precision gains depended on CP quality and validation rates, while small validation samples may affect confidence interval coverage. Conclusion: MAPS provides a flexible and efficient approach to EHR-based survival inference by combining limited chart-reviewed data with error-prone CPs across different validation patterns.

abstract: Psychiatric diagnosis depends on the clinician's ability to infer mental states from complex and dynamically evolving interpersonal signals. During the psychiatric interview, clinicians do not only collect explicit symptoms; they continuously sample a rich array of non-verbal and paralinguistic cues including gaze, prosody, affective reciprocity, and interactional timing. These signals are central to psychiatric assessment, yet their contribution to diagnostic reasoning remains poorly formalized. In this Review, we propose a computational account of clinical impressions in psychiatry. We integrate evidence from phenomenological psychopathology, social cognition, and computational neuroscience. We argue that such impressions may arise when the clinician's generative model of social interaction is persistently disconfirmed by subtle deviations in interpersonal behaviour, generating high-level social prediction errors experienced as a sense of incongruity or failed attunement. We formalize this process as VIBE: Violation of Interpersonal Bayesian Expectation. VIBE denotes a pre-reflective epistemic signal generated when observed interpersonal cues deviate from the clinician's expected model of social reciprocity. It is not a diagnostic criterion but orients hypothesis generation by drawing attention to disturbances in interpersonal predictability. We hypothesize that VIBE may constitute a transdiagnostic mechanism: different disorders, from schizophrenia to autism spectrum disorder and mood disorders, may disrupt distinct dimensions of interpersonal prediction. The Praecox Feeling, first described by Rümke in 1942, can be read as the earliest clinical formalization of this process and as its schizophrenia-spectrum instance, in which the profile of interpersonal violations is consistent enough to be clinically recognizable. This framework recasts the diagnostic impression as an embodied inferential process rather than an opaque subjective faculty. Teaching clinicians to articulate, examine, and recalibrate these impressions could strengthen diagnostic reasoning, reduce bias, and improve therapeutic attunement. VIBE provides a bridge between phenomenological psychopathology and computational neuroscience, and offers a tractable, empirically testable model for studying the neurocomputational basis of psychiatric clinical judgement.

abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 10 14 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

abstract: During early B cell development, pre-B cells encounter signaling from pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR) and DNA damage responses (DDR) triggered by RAG-induced DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) generated during immunoglobulin light chain (Igl) recombination. These signals drive cooperative and antagonistic programs to promote pre-B cell checkpoint. Here, we show in vivo that pre-B cells transition between distinct subpopulations predominated by either pre-BCR or RAG DSB-induced DDR signals. DDR initiates early in pre-B cells undergoing Igl recombination then drives cellular programming during terminal pre-B stages. We find that RAG DSB-induced DDR regulates coordinated pre-B cell differentiation, in part, by activation of the transcriptional repressor complex SPIC/BCLAF1. Loss of BCLAF1 disrupts pre-B cell developmental progression resulting in concomitant expression of pre-BCR and DDR programs with breakdown in segregation of clonal expansion and Igl recombination. These studies show that RAG DSB-induced DDR and BCLAF1 preserve pre-B cell checkpoint integrity in vivo during Igl recombination.
